blocks.h: (a) Preparation and trials before offering the ship for survey
1. Establish the ship's status before touching a machine

blocks.p: Reactivation begins on paper. I would establish, and put in one folder: the lay-up record (what was preserved, when, and by what method); every outstanding Condition of Class, memorandum and statutory deficiency; the survey and certificate status - which surveys fell due during lay-up and which certificates have expired; the repair specification and the yard's completed-work list with material and welding certificates; and the state of the planned maintenance system, which will have accrued a backlog. This tells me what the surveyor will ask for and what I must prove.

blocks.h: 2. Remove preservation and restore the systems that were shut down

blocks.p: Then, system by system: drain and renew preservation oils and dehumidification media; remove blanks, plugs and desiccant bags against the register that recorded them - the register is the control, not memory; re-fill and vent cooling, lubricating and fuel systems; renew or filter and test lubricating and hydraulic oils and system fuel after long standing; restore sea suctions, overboard valves and ship-side fittings and prove them tight; and re-establish the bilge, ballast and fire main.

blocks.h: 3. Static checks on machinery, boilers, electrical and auxiliary systems

blocks.p: Before anything is started: crankcase and gear inspection, turning gear rotation and clearance checks; insulation-resistance tests on every machine and the main and emergency switchboards, with results recorded against the lay-up readings; battery and UPS capacity; boiler internal examination, gauge glasses, safety valves and water treatment; steering gear internal and hydraulic checks; and calibration of pressure gauges, thermometers and instrumentation.

This is where a reactivation survey most often fails. Service and re-certify life-saving and fire-fighting appliances, breathing apparatus, fixed extinguishing systems and quick-closing valves; prove emergency generator, emergency fire pump, emergency lighting and the emergency steering; test fire and gas detection, watertight doors and remote stops; and re-commission the oily water separator with its 15 ppm alarm and stopping device, the sewage plant and the incinerator, with the record books brought up to date.

blocks.h: 5. Harbour trials - prove alongside everything that can be proved alongside

blocks.p: Run every auxiliary on load; parallel and load-share the generators and carry out a blackout and dead-ship recovery test; run the main engine on the turning gear, then air-blast, then a short ahead and astern trial on the moorings with the shaft brake and locking arrangement removed and the propeller clear; prove bridge, engine-control-room and local control positions and the changeover between them; test the engineers' alarm, telegraph and both means of bridge-to-engine-room communication; and run the steering gear through the full hard-over to hard-over test on both power units.

blocks.h: 6. Sea trials - what can only be proved under way

blocks.p: At sea, and with the Master, run a progressive load-up of the main engine with performance and indicator readings, exhaust temperature deviations and turbocharger condition logged; carry out crash-stop, ahead-astern and manoeuvring trials and the steering-gear trial under way; prove governor, overspeed trip and all shutdowns and slowdowns by actual test where the maker's procedure allows; take bearing temperatures, vibration and crankshaft deflections after the engine has come up to temperature; and hold the engine at service load long enough for a leak, an alarm or a temperature drift to declare itself before the surveyor is aboard.

blocks.h: 7. What is put in front of the surveying authority

blocks.p: The surveyor is shown evidence, not assurances: completed repair reports and material certificates; trial records signed and dated; insulation, calibration and safety-valve test sheets; the planned maintenance system restored and current; the oil record book, garbage record book and other statutory records in order; and a clear list of anything still outstanding with its plan and date. Anything I cannot prove, I declare - a defect found by me is a finding, a defect found by the surveyor is a deficiency.

blocks.h: (b) The effect of a laid-up notation on the survey cycle
8. What the notation does while the ship is laid up, and what happens on reactivation

blocks.p: Under class rules, a ship laid up in accordance with the Society's own lay-up requirements is held in a recognised lay-up condition rather than in normal service, and the effect is one of postponement, not cancellation:

rows: Annual
Falls due but is generally held in abeyance; class is not suspended merely because it becomes overdue, provided the lay-up was properly declared and the Society's lay-up conditions are kept.
Carried out as part of the reactivation survey.
Intermediate
Likewise held in abeyance. The intermediate window does not run in the ship's favour - the requirement survives the lay-up.
Carried out if its due date passed, or its window has opened, during the lay-up.
Special / renewal

The strongest effect. Class is generally maintained without survey only up to the special survey due date. Beyond it the Society typically assigns a notation such as 'Laid-Up Surveys Overdue' and requires minimum lay-up condition surveys to hold even that.

The postponed special survey must be carried out. Its scope is set by the requirements at the ORIGINAL due date, not by the ship's age when it is completed, and it is credited from the date originally due.

blocks.p: Three consequences follow. Lay-up condition surveys replace the normal cycle while the ship is idle - typically tightness of hull, stern gland and sea connections and confirmation that the lay-up conditions are maintained. A reactivation survey is required before return to service: where no due dates passed, a survey of annual scope; where they did, the postponed surveys themselves, plus clearance of any Condition of Class. And the lay-up buys no time overall - because credit runs from the original due date, the five-year cycle is not pushed out by the idle period. Finally, class lay-up does not extend a statutory certificate: SOLAS, Load Line and MARPOL certification is the Administration's business, and the flag State - in India, under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 - must be approached separately.

Limb (a) is worth 10 and limb (b) is worth 6, so roughly two-thirds of the writing belongs to the reactivation. The mark-winning move in (a) is to separate preparation from trials and then to separate harbour trials from sea trials, because that is the examiner's own word order and it gives four countable blocks instead of one long list. Limb (b) is short and specific: three named surveys, three answers. Do not turn it into a general essay on classification.

Lay-up postpones; it does not forgive. Everything in limb (b) falls out of that one sentence. The requirement survives the idle period, the survey is done on reactivation, and - the point most candidates miss - the scope and credit of a postponed special survey are fixed by the original due date, not by how old the ship is when it is finally surveyed. A ship laid up for two years does not get a two-year holiday from her five-year cycle.

blocks.h: Why the answer says 'under class rules' rather than naming a rule

blocks.p: The lay-up regime is a classification-society regime, not a convention one. No SOLAS regulation and no IMO resolution creates a laid-up notation. The shape above is common across societies - abeyance, condition surveys, an overdue notation, a reactivation survey, credit from the original due date - but the trigger periods, the notation wording and the additional time allowed before disclassing differ between them. In the exam, state the mechanism and attribute it to the Society's rules; do not quote a period as though it were universal.

ul: Answering (a) with a preservation list. That is the other question - how to lay a ship UP. This one is about proving her fit to come back.

Going to sea trials without harbour trials. The examiner has asked for 'trials' in a survey context, and a moored ahead-and-astern trial, a blackout recovery and a hard-over steering test are all scoring items that cost no sea time.

Forgetting that reactivation defects cluster in emergency and pollution-prevention equipment - emergency generator, emergency fire pump, OWS 15 ppm alarm - because those are the systems nobody ran during the lay-up.
Saying the laid-up notation cancels or resets surveys. It postpones them.
Saying a postponed special survey is done to the requirements for the ship's age on the day it is completed. It is done to the requirements at the original due date and credited from that date.
Assuming class lay-up carries the statutory certificates with it. It does not - flag State and RO are a separate approach.
Removing blanks and plugs from memory instead of from the register that recorded them.

blocks.p:
"Your ship was laid up for eighteen months and the special survey fell due in month six. What is her class status?" Not automatically suspended if she was properly laid up under the Society's rules - but past the special survey due date she is typically carrying an overdue-surveys notation, held by minimum lay-up condition surveys, and she cannot trade until the postponed special survey is completed.

"Which trial would you not skip, and why?" The steering gear hard-over test and the ahead-astern trial - both are required before departure in normal service anyway, both prove control rather than condition, and both are what the surveyor will ask to witness.

"Who tells you the ship may trade again - class or flag?" Both, separately. Class reinstates classification on completion of the reactivation surveys; the Administration or its RO deals with the statutory certificates.

ul: What is a lay-up condition survey, and what does it usually cover? Tightness of hull, stern gland and sea connections, and confirmation that the declared lay-up conditions are being maintained.
What determines the scope of a postponed special survey? The requirements at the original due date, not the ship's age at completion.
Name three trials you would run alongside. Blackout and dead-ship recovery, moored ahead-and-astern engine trial, steering gear hard-over to hard-over.
What insulation reading would concern you on reactivation? Any machine that has fallen materially below its recorded lay-up value - long standing with heaters off draws in moisture.
Does lay-up extend the certificate validity? No. Class postponement and statutory certificate validity are different things.

blocks.p: Two limits are declared in the answer rather than hidden. First, the lay-up survey detail is society-specific: the length of lay-up that triggers a condition survey, its interval, the exact notation and the extra period allowed before disclassing all differ, so the answer gives the mechanism and attributes the detail to the Society's rules. Second, the statutory position is flag-specific: the answer states only that class lay-up does not of itself extend a statutory certificate, and does not assert any Administration's practice on extension or re-issue. questions.understand_first: Two different jobs are hiding in one question. The first is practical: a ship that has been sitting still for a long time is not a ship that is merely switched off. Oil drains away from surfaces, moisture works into windings, seals take a set, and the systems nobody ever ran while she was idle - the emergency generator, the emergency fire pump, the oily water separator - are exactly the ones that will not start when you need them. So the job is not to inspect her, it is to prove her, and you prove her in a deliberate order: read the paperwork first so you know what was done to her, undo the protection you or somebody else put on, check what can be checked while everything is stopped, then run her - first tied to the quay where a failure costs nothing, then at sea where the load is real. Only then do you invite the surveyor, and what you hand him is evidence, not confidence. The second job is a rules question with a counter-intuitive answer. Putting a ship into a declared idle state does not make her survey obligations go away, and it does not restart her clock. It parks them. When she wakes up, everything that fell due while she slept has to be done, and the big five-yearly examination is done to the standard that applied on the day it was originally owed - not the softer or harder standard that would apply on the day you finally get round to it. Idle time buys no time.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a laid-up notation cancel, reset or postpone the periodical surveys?
retrieval_cards.answer: It postpones them. Annual and intermediate surveys are held in abeyance while the ship is properly laid up under the Society's rules, and are carried out on reactivation. Nothing is cancelled and the cycle is not reset.
retrieval_cards.why: This one word governs the whole of limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a postponed special survey scoped and credited?
retrieval_cards.answer: To the requirements that applied at its ORIGINAL due date, not to the ship's age when it is finally completed, and it is credited from the date originally due.
retrieval_cards.why: So a long lay-up buys no extension of the five-year cycle.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to class if the lay-up runs past the special survey due date?
retrieval_cards.answer: Class is generally maintained without survey only up to that date. Beyond it the Society typically assigns an overdue-surveys notation and requires minimum lay-up condition surveys - broadly tightness of hull, stern gland and sea connections - to hold even that status.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the harbour trials you would run before offering the ship for survey.
retrieval_cards.answer: Auxiliaries on load and generators paralleled; a blackout and dead-ship recovery test; a moored ahead-and-astern main engine trial with the shaft locking removed; all three control positions and their changeover; the engineers' alarm and both bridge communication means; and steering gear hard-over to hard-over on both power units.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which systems most often fail a reactivation survey, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: The emergency and pollution-prevention systems - emergency generator, emergency fire pump, emergency lighting and steering, and the oily water separator with its 15 ppm alarm - because they are the systems that were never run during the lay-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does class lay-up extend the statutory certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The laid-up regime is a classification-society regime; SOLAS, Load Line and MARPOL certification is the Administration's business and must be taken up separately with the flag State or its recognized organization.
retrieval_cards.why: No SOLAS regulation and no IMO resolution creates a laid-up notation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why remove blanks and plugs against a register rather than by inspection?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a blank left in a sea suction, a vent or an exhaust is invisible once the space is closed up and is only discovered on load. The register that recorded them going in is the control for taking them out.

blocks.h: 1. The exchange with the Master, and the information the dock requires

blocks.p: Docking is a joint operation and the Master carries the ship. What I give him: the docking plan and shell expansion, the approved docking condition (draught fore and aft and the trim I need), the tank plan with the intended state of every tank, the work list and its critical path, the machinery that must remain available and until when, and any defect, damage or Condition of Class that bears on entry. What I ask him for: the confirmed dock date and tide window, the dock's own entry conditions, the ballast and trim he needs for the passage in, the cargo and slop position, and the crew and watch arrangements ashore. Between us we settle one thing above all - the stability condition on entry, because the ship must be upright and at a controlled trim and must have adequate stability at the moment of taking the blocks.

blocks.h: 2. Condition of the ship for docking - draught, trim, stability and tanks

blocks.p: The ship enters with no list and with the small stern trim the dock requires so that she takes the after keel blocks first. Free surface is minimised: tanks are pressed up or run dry, not left slack, because free surface bites hardest in the critical period between touching the blocks and taking the full weight, when the effective metacentric height is being reduced by the block reaction. Bunkers, fresh water, ballast and slops are set to the agreed figures and soundings taken and recorded immediately before entry. Any tank to be opened, gas-freed or repaired is emptied and cleaned in advance.

blocks.h: 3. Preparing the machinery and services for shutdown

blocks.p: Arrange the changeover from ship's services to shore services - shore power, shore fresh water, shore fire main connection and the international shore connection - so nothing is lost in the gap. Prepare for the loss of sea water: the main engine, generators, air conditioning and refrigeration all lose their cooling once the dock is pumped down, so agree which will run on shore-supplied cooling and which will stop. Have bilge and drainage arrangements agreed with the dock, since gravity drainage overboard is available in dock and must be controlled. Sound and record all tanks, secure the boiler, and prepare the propeller shaft locking or turning arrangement so the shaft cannot rotate with the dock flow.

blocks.h: 4. Delegation of responsibilities to the engineers

blocks.p: Every task gets a name, not a department:

rows: Second Engineer
Overall in-dock work programme, main engine and shafting work, block-to-block coordination of the engine-room work list, and the plug register.
Third Engineer
Sea suctions, sea chests, overboard valves, ship-side fittings and their gratings; boiler and auxiliary boiler work.
Fourth Engineer
Bilge, ballast and fire main systems, pumps and their strainers; sounding and recording of tanks.
Electro-technical Officer

Shore power changeover and its earthing, hull-mounted equipment - echo sounder, speed log and transducers - cathodic protection anodes and impressed-current system, and isolation of anything that must not be energised.
All engineers
Permit-to-work discipline, enclosed-space entry, hot-work control and fire watch in their own area.

blocks.p: Delegation is of task, not of accountability: I retain responsibility, so each officer reports completion to me against a signed list.

blocks.h: 5. Entering the dock and taking the blocks

blocks.p: During entry the engine room is manned and the main engine and steering are available until the dock master releases them. The ship is centred on the dock centreline against the docking plan block layout; divers or the dock check the fore-and-aft and athwartship position before the water is dropped. Once she is on the blocks the propeller shaft is locked, the rudder secured amidships, and the water pumped down in stages with the ship watched for movement or list.

blocks.h: 6. In dock - services, safety and the plug and valve regime

blocks.p: Bottom plugs are drawn only against a written register, and the drawn plugs are landed in one controlled place - the single commonest cause of a flooded engine room on refloating is a plug that was never refitted. Sea suctions and overboard valves are opened for cleaning, examination and gauging with their blanks fitted and tagged. Anodes are renewed, the stern tube and rudder clearances (poker gauge and jumping-bar readings) taken and recorded with the class surveyor, and tailshaft, propeller and rudder examined. Fire and safety in dock is a joint regime: hot-work permits, gas-free certificates, fire watches, unobstructed gangways and escape routes, and the shore fire main connected and pressurised.

blocks.h: 7. Inspections and co-operation with the dock authority before undocking

blocks.p: Nothing is flooded up until a joint ship-and-dock pre-undocking inspection has walked the bottom and signed for it. The inspection confirms: every plug refitted, torqued and witnessed against the register; all ship-side valves and blanks correctly restored and their positions logged; sea chest gratings refitted; anodes secured; propeller, rudder and stern gear complete with the clearances recorded and the class surveyor's attendance closed out; echo sounder and log transducers refitted and their fairings faired; all staging, scaffolding, tools and debris removed from the dock bottom and from sea chests; paint work cured; and the hull free of any opening not accounted for. In parallel we agree with the dock the undocking condition - draughts, trim, tank state and stability - and confirm class and statutory attendance is complete and any Condition of Class cleared.

blocks.h: 8. Flooding up, undocking and restoration to service

blocks.p: During flooding the engine room is manned and all bilges, tank tops, sea chest spaces and the shaft tunnel are physically watched for leakage, with pumps ready; flooding is stopped at once if anything is found. When she lifts, soundings are retaken, the shaft unlocked and turned, machinery restarted in a controlled sequence and cooling water proved, steering gear tested hard-over to hard-over, and shore services released only when ship's services have taken the load. Before departure the Master and I confirm the ship's readiness for sea: engine trials ahead and astern, control from all three positions, communications, and the record of everything done handed over for the survey and maintenance record.

This is one 16-mark question containing four separate demands, and the examiner has signalled them with four verbs - state the coordination with the Master, list the preparations, state the delegation, enlist the undocking inspections. Marks are almost certainly split across all four. The commonest failure is a long, well-informed preparation list that never mentions the Master, never names an engineer, and stops at the moment the dock is pumped down. Answer chronologically - before, entry, in dock, before undocking, undocking - and all four limbs get covered in their natural place.

blocks.h: The stability point that carries the docking condition

blocks.p: The dangerous moment in docking is not when the ship is sitting on the blocks; it is the interval between touching the after blocks and taking her full weight. As the water goes down, the blocks push up with a force P at the keel, and that upward force acts exactly like removing weight from the bottom of the ship - it reduces the effective GM. If she has a list, or slack tanks adding free surface, or too much trim so that P builds up over a long period on one point, she can become unstable and slip. That is why the answer insists on upright, minimum free surface and a small controlled stern trim. If you can say why, rather than just what, this paragraph is worth real marks.

blocks.h: The two things that actually sink ships on refloating

blocks.p: A plug that was never refitted, and a sea valve left open with its blank removed. Both are register problems, not skill problems, which is exactly why the answer makes the plug register and the joint pre-undocking inspection formal, signed steps rather than a walk-round. Write the register into your answer explicitly - it is the difference between a checklist and a control.

blocks.h: Operational practice is not statute - keep them apart

blocks.p: Almost nothing in this answer is prescribed by an international instrument. There is no SOLAS regulation on how to dock a ship. What the instruments do supply is the framework: the ISM Code requires the Company to establish procedures for key shipboard operations and for maintenance (elements 7 and 10) and fixes the Master's authority (element 5); SOLAS chapter I regulation 11 requires the condition to be maintained after survey and defects to be reported; and class rules require attendance and approval for repairs affecting class, and set the bottom-survey requirement that is usually the reason for the docking in the first place. Say which is which. Presenting dock practice as though it were regulation is a marked error.

ul: Writing only the preparation limb. There are four demands and three of them are not preparation.
Never naming an engineer. 'Delegation of responsibilities' means Second, Third, Fourth and ETO with a task each - a departmental sentence does not answer it.
Leaving tanks slack. Free surface is at its most damaging in the critical period, and a slack tank in a docking condition is a fault, not a neutral choice.
Entering with a list. She must be upright.
Forgetting the transducers. Echo sounder and speed log fairings are hull openings and belong on both the removal and the refitting list.
Forgetting to lock the shaft, or unlocking it before the ship is fully afloat.
Treating undocking as the reverse of docking with no separate inspection. The joint pre-undocking inspection is a scoring limb in its own right.
Releasing shore services before ship's services have taken the load.

blocks.p:
"Why does the ship need a stern trim entering the dock?" So that she lands on the after blocks first and settles progressively forward along the keel, rather than landing bodily and unpredictably. The trim must be small and controlled - excessive trim concentrates the block reaction at one point for longer and makes the critical period worse.

"Who is responsible for the plugs?" I am. The Second Engineer holds the register as a delegated task, but delegation transfers the task and never the accountability - which is also the ISM Code's own position on the Master's and the Company's responsibilities.

"You find a crack in a propeller blade in dock. What changes?" The Company and the classification society are informed at once, and no repair is started until the repair procedure is approved and attendance arranged - the same discipline as any repair affecting class.

ul: What information does the dock master need from you? The docking plan and block layout, the shell expansion showing every ship-side opening, the docking draughts and trim, the tank condition and the ship's displacement.
Which readings are taken with the surveyor in dock? Tailshaft and stern tube clearances by poker gauge, rudder pintle and jumping-bar clearances, and propeller condition.
What is the international shore connection for? To allow the shore fire main to supply the ship's fire main when the ship's own pumps are unavailable.
What are you watching during flooding up? Every bilge, tank top, sea chest space and the shaft tunnel, for leakage, with pumps ready and flooding stopped at once if any is found.

Where does the ISM Code touch this operation? Element 7 procedures for key shipboard operations, element 10 maintenance, element 5 the Master's authority, element 8 emergency preparedness for the in-dock fire regime.

blocks.p: Run the clock: TALK - TRIM - SHUT DOWN - DELEGATE - LAND - WORK - INSPECT - FLOOD (steps 1 to 8). Within the work and inspect steps, one word covers the danger: PLUGS. Register out, register in, signed by two people.

SOLAS chapter I regulation 11 - maintenance of condition after survey and reporting of accidents or defects.

questions.understand_first: A dry dock is the one operation where the ship stops being a floating object and becomes a supported one, and almost everything that matters follows from that changeover. While she is settling onto the blocks she is neither properly afloat nor properly landed: the blocks push up on her keel, and pushing up on the bottom of a ship has the same effect as taking weight out of the bottom of her - she gets less stable, not more. That is why she must go in upright, with a small deliberate stern trim so she lands progressively rather than all at once, and with no half-full tanks sloshing about making it worse. It is also why this is not something an engineer arranges alone: the person responsible for the ship's condition and safety is the Master, and the person who knows what the machinery, the tanks and the hull openings will be doing is you, so the two of you have to hand each other the halves of the same picture. Once she is landed, the whole ship is opened up - plugs out of the bottom, valves off, gratings off, transducers out - and the single fact that matters is that every one of those openings has to go back. That is a bookkeeping problem, not an engineering one, which is why it is answered with a register and a joint signed inspection rather than with skill. And undocking is not docking played backwards: it has its own inspection, and its own watch on every space that could take water, because the first minutes of flooding are when a missing plug tells you it is missing.

blocks.h: (a) The primary objective of the Hague and Hague-Visby Rules
1. The problem the Rules were created to solve

blocks.p: Before the Rules, carriage was governed by freedom of contract, and the carrier drafted the bill of lading. Exclusion clauses grew until the carrier had contracted out of almost every liability, including his own negligence. The cargo owner, the endorsee and the bank financing the shipment held a document that promised very little and could not be relied on across jurisdictions, so goods and credit both became harder to move. National legislatures began to intervene separately, which threatened to fragment the law of the bill of lading.

The primary objective is to impose a uniform, mandatory minimum standard of carrier liability on contracts of carriage covered by a bill of lading, so that the risk of loss or damage to cargo is allocated between carrier and cargo interest in a way that neither can contract out of, and is allocated the same way in every contracting State. Two words carry it: minimum, because the carrier may always assume more but never less; and uniform, because the value of the bill of lading depends on it meaning the same thing wherever it is presented. The commercial purpose behind both is certainty - a bargain both sides can price and insure.

blocks.h: 3. How the objective is delivered - the two halves of the bargain

blocks.p: The Rules are a bargain, not a code of protection, and an answer that gives only the cargo half has missed the objective.

headers: What the carrier gets in return
rows: Due diligence, before and at the beginning of the voyage, to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the cargo spaces fit and safe (Schedule Article III(1))
A closed list of excepted perils - headed by act, neglect or default in the navigation or management of the ship, and by fire (Article IV(2))
To properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods (Article III(2))
A limitation of liability - 666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is higher (Article IV(5))

To issue on demand a bill of lading showing marks, quantity and apparent order and condition, which is prima facie evidence and becomes conclusive in the hands of a good-faith transferee (Article III(3) and (4))
A short time bar - suit within one year of delivery or of the date when the goods should have been delivered (Article III(6))
The anti-avoidance rule: any clause relieving or lessening liability otherwise than as the Rules provide is null and void (Article III(8))
Freedom from the Rules in a charterparty, which remains a matter of negotiation between commercial equals (Article V)

blocks.h: 4. What the Protocols added, and the Indian position at this sitting

blocks.p:
The Visby Protocol 1968 and the SDR Protocol 1979 did not change the objective; they repaired the machinery that was failing to deliver it. The package limitation had been eroded by inflation and by containerisation, so limitation was recast on a package or weight basis whichever is higher, expressed in Special Drawing Rights, with an enumeration rule for containers and pallets; the bill was made conclusive against a good-faith transferee; and the limitation was lost for conduct intended to cause damage or reckless with knowledge that damage would probably result.

In India the Rules do not apply of their own force - they operate through statute, and that statute changed shortly before this sitting. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 came into force on 10 September 2025, repealing the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, and re-enacts the Rules with modifications in its Schedule. Its section 5 is a statutory clause paramount: every bill of lading issued in India must state expressly that it takes effect subject to the applicable rules. Two Indian modifications are worth knowing - the one-year bar carries a proviso allowing a further period of not more than three months as the court allows, and the definition of goods expressly includes live animals and cargo carried on deck. The Bills of Lading Act, 2025 replaced the 1856 Act on the same day.

blocks.h: (b) When cargo is abandoned, and who carries the liability
5. What abandonment means - and the three senses that must not be mixed

blocks.p: No carriage convention and no Indian carriage statute defines abandoned cargo. It is a description of a factual state - the person entitled to the goods has shown, by conduct or by declaration, that he will not take them - to which customs law, port regulation and the contract of carriage then attach consequences. It must be kept apart from two different things that share the word: abandonment to the insurer, which is the notice of abandonment given on a constructive total loss under marine insurance law and transfers the proprietary interest to the underwriter; and abandonment of the ship as a wreck, which is a merchant shipping and wreck-removal question. This question is about the first.

blocks.h: 6. The circumstances in which cargo is treated as abandoned

ul: Non-collection. The consignee does not present himself, or presents no original bill of lading, within a reasonable time or within the period the port or customs allows.
Economic abandonment - the commonest cause. Accrued demurrage, detention, storage and duty exceed the value of the goods, so nobody has an economic reason to claim them.
Rejection under the sale contract - the buyer refuses the goods for quality, quantity, delay or a fallen market, and the seller is unwilling to take them back.
Regulatory refusal - import licence refused, goods prohibited, failed sanitary or phytosanitary inspection, or seizure by customs.
Condition of the goods - perished, contaminated, damaged beyond commercial value, or dangerous or misdeclared cargo which no one will own.
Insolvency or disappearance of the consignee, or a documentary failure that leaves nobody able to prove title.

Formal relinquishment in Indian law. Under section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 the owner of imported goods may, at any time before an order for clearance or warehousing, relinquish his title, and is then not liable for the duty - except where an offence appears to have been committed, in which case relinquishment is not allowed. This is abandonment as a legal act rather than as a fact.

Statutory non-clearance. Under section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962, goods not cleared for home consumption, warehoused or transhipped within thirty days of unloading - or where title has been relinquished - may, after notice to the importer and with the permission of the proper officer, be sold by the person having custody. Animals, perishable and hazardous goods may be sold at any time with that permission.

blocks.p: The important point is that liability does not disappear when the goods are abandoned. Abandonment sheds the asset; it does not by itself shed the obligations.

rows: Consignee / cargo owner
Primarily liable. Failing to take delivery is a breach of the carriage contract, and he remains liable for freight, demurrage, detention, storage, disposal and any damage the cargo causes.
Shipper

Remains liable. Bills of lading almost always define 'Merchant' to include shipper, consignee, holder and receiver and make them jointly and severally liable, so the carrier can look back to the shipper when the consignee walks away. Under the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 the transfer of rights of suit to the consignee does not release the original shipper from freight.
Freight forwarder / NVOCC
Liable in his own right where he contracted as principal on the bill rather than as agent - a distinction that decides who the line sues.
Carrier / shipping line

Not the owner of the goods, but carries the practical exposure: he pays the terminal, the customs charges and the disposal, and recovers from the merchant if he can. He also remains a bailee of the goods and owes reasonable care until they are lawfully disposed of.
Terminal / custodian and customs

Hold the goods and, in India, hold the power of sale under section 48 after notice and with the proper officer's permission. Sale proceeds are applied to duty, charges and freight, with any surplus dealt with as the law directs.

blocks.p: In practice the carrier: gives written notice to the merchant and sets a deadline; exercises the contractual lien on the goods for freight, general average and charges; discharges and warehouses at the merchant's risk and expense under the bill's liberty clauses; keeps the demurrage clock and the evidence, because the claim will be for accrued charges; obtains customs and port authority permission and then sells or destroys the goods, crediting the proceeds; and pursues the merchant, jointly and severally, for the shortfall - notifying the P&I club or cargo liability insurer early. Where the cargo is dangerous or misdeclared, the carrier's position is stronger still, because the shipper's undertaking as to the nature of the goods is broken.

Limb (a) asks for an objective, not a syllabus. The temptation is to write out Article III and Article IV and hope the objective emerges; it does not, and it burns half the paper. State the objective in one proposition first - a uniform, mandatory minimum allocation of cargo risk that neither party can contract out of - then show it working through the two halves of the bargain. The table earns its place because it makes the reciprocity visible in one glance. Limb (b) is two questions with equal weight: when, and who. Give a list for the first and a table for the second, and make sure the answer says plainly that liability does not vanish with the goods.

blocks.h: The statute book moved, and it moved recently

blocks.p: This is the single most important currency point on the question. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 and the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 came into force on 10 September 2025, repealing the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 and the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 respectively. Almost every textbook, note set and older solved answer in circulation still writes the 1925 Act. For a sitting in August 2026 that is a repealed statute. Name the 2025 Acts, mention the statutory clause paramount in section 5, and you have said something a candidate working from stale material cannot say.

blocks.h: Minimum, not maximum - the idea most answers miss

blocks.p: The Rules fix a floor. A carrier may agree to greater liability than the Rules impose, and that agreement is perfectly good; what he may not do is agree to less, because Article III(8) makes any such clause null and void. This one-way character is what makes the regime mandatory minimum rather than a standard-form contract, and it explains the anti-avoidance rule, the statutory clause paramount and the deeming of a benefit-of-insurance clause as an attempt to lessen liability.

The word does three jobs in maritime law and mixing them is the classic error in limb (b). Abandonment of cargo - the consignee will not take the goods; a commercial fact with customs and contractual consequences. Abandonment to the underwriter - notice of abandonment on a constructive total loss under marine insurance law, which transfers the insured's proprietary interest to the insurer on acceptance. Abandonment of the ship - the owner walks away from a wreck, which raises wreck removal and merchant shipping duties. If the question says cargo, answer on the first and mention the others only to show you know they are different.

ul: Answering limb (a) by reciting the articles. The objective is a proposition; the articles are evidence for it.
Giving only the cargo-protection half. The Rules are a bargain - defences, limitation and the one-year bar are part of the objective, not exceptions to it.
Writing the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925. It was repealed with effect from 10 September 2025, eleven months before this sitting.
Bringing in the Hamburg Rules as Indian law. India is not a party to them.

Saying that on abandonment the goods become the carrier's problem and the merchant is free. He is not - the merchant remains liable for freight, demurrage, storage and disposal, and the bill's Merchant clause usually makes shipper and consignee jointly and severally liable.
Confusing abandonment of cargo with notice of abandonment to an underwriter, or with abandonment of a wreck.
Asserting a rupee limitation figure. The unit of account is the Special Drawing Right and no conversion is given here.
Treating the thirty-day period in section 48 of the Customs Act as a definition of abandonment. It is a trigger for the custodian's power of sale, which is not the same thing.

blocks.p:
"If the Rules protect cargo, why do they give the carrier a defence for negligent navigation?" Because the objective is an allocation of risk, not the maximisation of carrier liability. The nautical fault defence was the price of getting carriers to accept a non-excludable seaworthiness obligation and a mandatory floor at all. The Hamburg Rules later removed it - and India is not a party.

"Can a carrier agree to more liability than the Rules impose?" Yes. The Rules set a minimum. Only clauses that lessen liability are struck down.

"The consignee has vanished and the box is full of rotting fruit. What do you do first?" Notice to the merchant, then customs - perishables can be sold at any time with the proper officer's permission under section 48, so the clock and the condition of the goods drive the sequence, and the lien is preserved throughout.

ul: Which Act gives the Rules effect in India today? The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025, in force 10 September 2025, which repealed the 1925 Act.
What is a statutory clause paramount? Section 5 of the 2025 Act - every bill of lading issued in India must state expressly that it takes effect subject to the applicable rules.
What is the Hague-Visby package limitation? 666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is higher.
How long has a cargo claimant got? One year, with an Indian proviso allowing a further period of not more than three months as the court allows.

Under which section may uncleared imported goods be sold in India, and after how long? Section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962, after thirty days from unloading, on notice to the importer and with the permission of the proper officer.
Does relinquishing title escape the duty? Under section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 yes - unless an offence appears to have been committed.

blocks.p: For (a): MINIMUM - UNIFORM - MUTUAL. A floor the carrier cannot go below, the same floor everywhere, in exchange for defences, a limit and a short clock. For (b): WHY - WHO. Why cargo is abandoned reduces to nobody wants it, nobody may have it, or nobody can be found; who pays reduces to the merchant owes it, the carrier fronts it, the custodian sells it.

ul: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), in force 10 September 2025 - gives effect in India to the Hague Rules as amended by the 1968 and 1979 Protocols, with modifications set out in its Schedule. Section 4 no implied absolute undertaking of seaworthiness; section 5 statutory clause paramount; section 12(1) repeal of the 1925 Act.

COGSA 2025 Schedule - Article III(1) due diligence, III(2) care of cargo, III(3) and (4) the bill as receipt and evidence, III(6) one-year bar with the Indian three-month judicial extension, III(8) anti-avoidance; Article IV(1) burden of proof, IV(2) excepted perils, IV(4) reasonable deviation, IV(5) limitation; Article V charterparties.

Customs Act, 1962 section 23(2) - relinquishment of title, with the offence proviso; section 48 - sale of goods not cleared within thirty days, or where title is relinquished.
Hamburg Rules 1978 - India is not a party. Rotterdam Rules 2008 - not in force.
'Abandoned cargo' has no statutory definition in the carriage legislation; the consequences come from customs law, port regulation and the contract of carriage.

blocks.p: Three limits are stated openly. First, the article content used here is taken from the Schedule to the Indian Act of 2025 as published in the Gazette, and not from the text of the international Hague or Visby instruments. The Act gives the Rules effect with modifications, so where the two might differ this answer speaks of the Indian Schedule - which is the right choice for an Indian examination, but is worth knowing if you meet the international text elsewhere. Second, 'abandoned cargo' is not a legal term of art - it has no definition in any carriage convention or in the 2025 Act - and the answer says so rather than offering a definition with false authority. Third, no case law is relied on on either limb; the boundary between management of the ship and care of cargo, and the effect of a Merchant clause, are described as settled commercial practice without citing decided authority.

questions.understand_first: Start with the commercial problem, because the answer to the first half is just the solution to it. If the person who carries your goods is also the person who writes the contract, he will keep writing until he owes you nothing - and that is exactly what happened. The trouble is that this does not only hurt the cargo owner; it destroys the usefulness of the shipping document itself, because a bank asked to lend money against a piece of paper needs to know what that paper is worth, and a piece of paper promising nothing is worth nothing. So the fix was not to make the carrier liable for everything. It was to take the pen away from him for one specific part of the contract: to fix a floor of responsibility he cannot write himself out of, and to fix the same floor in every country so the document means one thing wherever it is presented. In exchange the carrier was given something real - a defined list of situations where he is not liable, a cap on what he can be made to pay, and a short window in which he can be sued at all. It is a settlement between two industries, not a protection statute, and the give and the take are both part of the objective. The second half is about a much more ordinary situation. Goods arrive and nobody comes for them - because the buyer has changed his mind, or the market has fallen, or the storage bill has quietly grown larger than the cargo is worth. The instinctive answer is that walking away ends the matter. It does not. Walking away from a thing does not walk you away from the promises you made about it, and somebody still has to pay the port, feed the reefer and eventually get rid of it.

retrieval_cards.answer: 666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is higher. Suit within one year, with an Indian proviso allowing a further period of not more than three months as the court allows.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three different things called 'abandonment' in maritime law.
retrieval_cards.answer: Abandonment of cargo - the consignee will not take the goods. Abandonment to the underwriter - notice of abandonment on a constructive total loss, transferring the proprietary interest to the insurer. Abandonment of the ship - the owner walks away from a wreck, raising wreck removal duties.
retrieval_cards.why: Mixing them is the classic error in this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does abandoning cargo end the merchant's liability?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Abandonment sheds the asset, not the obligations. The consignee remains liable for freight, demurrage, detention, storage and disposal, and the bill's Merchant clause normally makes shipper, consignee and holder jointly and severally liable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does Indian customs law provide about uncleared and relinquished cargo?
retrieval_cards.answer: Customs Act, 1962 section 23(2) lets the owner relinquish title before an order for clearance or warehousing, escaping duty, unless an offence appears to have been committed. Section 48 lets the custodian sell goods not cleared, warehoused or transhipped within thirty days of unloading, or whose title has been relinquished, after notice to the importer and with the proper officer's permission.
retrieval_cards.why: Perishable, hazardous goods and animals may be sold at any time with that permission.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the carrier do about an abandoned container?
retrieval_cards.answer: Notice to the merchant with a deadline; exercise the lien for freight, general average and charges; discharge and warehouse at the merchant's risk and expense; preserve the demurrage clock and the evidence; obtain customs and port permission and sell or destroy, crediting the proceeds; then pursue the merchant jointly and severally for the shortfall, notifying the liability insurer early.

blocks.h: 1. The statute, and one caution this question requires

blocks.p: The governing statute in India is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. The United Kingdom Act of 1906 is its model but is not operative here, and the English Insurance Act 2015 reform does not apply in India. One further caution decides how two of these notes must be written: the Act governs the contract of marine insurance, while the clauses of a policy are contractual. Deviation and warranties are creatures of the Act. A war risk clause and a charterers' contribution clause are creatures of the market, and it is an error to attribute them to a section of the Act because they appear in an insurance question.

Definition. A ship deviates when she departs from the course of the voyage contemplated by the policy - from the course specifically designated by the policy where there is one, and otherwise from the usual and customary course. Intention to deviate is immaterial; there must be a deviation in fact.

Effect. Where a ship deviates without lawful excuse, the insurer is discharged from liability as from the time of deviation - and it is immaterial that she had regained her route before any loss occurred. The insurer remains liable for losses occurring before the deviation.

Lawful excuses. Deviation or delay is excused where it is authorised by a special term of the policy; caused by circumstances beyond the control of the master and his employer; reasonably necessary to comply with an express or implied warranty; reasonably necessary for the safety of the ship or the subject-matter insured; for the purpose of saving human life or aiding a ship in distress where human life may be in danger; reasonably necessary to obtain medical or surgical aid for a person on board; or caused by the barratrous conduct of master or crew where barratry is an insured peril. When the excuse ceases the ship must resume her course with reasonable despatch.

Practical point. The insurance rule is narrower than the carriage rule. Under the carriage regime a reasonable deviation, including one to save property at sea, is not a breach; under the Act, saving property alone is not among the excuses - it must be human life, or a ship in distress where life may be in danger. A master may therefore be safe under the bill of lading and have prejudiced the policy.

Nature. A warranty in marine insurance is a promissory warranty by which the assured undertakes that some thing shall or shall not be done, or that a condition shall be fulfilled, or affirms or negatives the existence of a particular state of facts. Its severity is the opposite of the ordinary contractual sense: it is the severe term, not the minor one.

Effect. It must be exactly complied with, whether or not it is material to the risk. On breach the insurer is discharged from liability as from the date of the breach, without prejudice to any liability incurred before it - so the assured cannot cure the breach and revive the cover. Breach is excused only where a change of circumstances makes the warranty no longer applicable, or where compliance is rendered unlawful by a subsequent law; and the insurer may waive a breach.

Express and implied. An express warranty is written into or upon the policy, or contained in a document incorporated by reference - in a hull and machinery policy, typically a classification warranty, a navigation or trading limits warranty, or a lay-up warranty. An implied warranty arises by operation of law without being written: seaworthiness at the commencement of the voyage in a voyage policy, and legality of the adventure in every policy. The twist candidates miss: a time policy carries no implied warranty of seaworthiness, but where the ship is sent to sea in an unseaworthy state with the privity of the assured, the insurer is not liable for loss attributable to that unseaworthiness.

Jurisdiction. English law changed under the Insurance Act 2015, where breach now suspends cover. In India the consequence remains discharge.

Where it sits. The Act includes war-type perils within maritime perils - men-of-war, capture, seizure, restraint and detainment of princes and peoples. But the Act does not contain a war risk clause: it is a policy clause, and its practical effect is to define what the ordinary policy will not pay for.

What it does. The standard hull, machinery and cargo policy excludes war, civil war, revolution, insurrection, capture, seizure, arrest, restraint and detainment, derelict mines and torpedoes, and terrorism and malicious acts. Because the exclusion would otherwise leave the assured bare, the same perils are bought back separately under war risk cover - Institute war and strikes wordings on the hull and cargo side, and war risk protection and indemnity cover for the liability side.

How it operates. War risk cover is written on a different commercial basis from ordinary hull cover because the exposure moves: the market's war risk committee designates listed areas for which an additional premium is charged; the assured must notify entry into and departure from such an area, often with a limited number of days included; the cover is cancellable at short notice by either party as the political situation changes; and it terminates automatically on the outbreak of war between the major powers or on the hostile detonation of a nuclear weapon.

Why the Chief Engineer meets it. Because trading into a listed area triggers the notice, the additional premium, the crew's war bonus and the associated hardening measures, and because a detention or arrest is covered - if at all - by the war policy and not by the ordinary one.

State the position first. The Marine Insurance Act contains no clause of that name. Two settled ideas lie behind the phrase, and a good short note gives both.

Contribution as the Act uses the word. Contribution in the Act is the doctrine of double insurance: where the assured is over-insured because the same risk is covered by more than one policy, the assured may claim under any of them but cannot recover more than the indemnity, and each insurer is bound, as between the insurers, to contribute rateably in proportion to the amount for which he is liable. An insurer who pays more than his rateable proportion has a right of contribution against the others.

The charterer's contribution in general average. General average is a contribution by all the interests in the adventure to an extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure intentionally and reasonably made for the common safety. Ship and cargo are the obvious contributors, but a charterer commonly has property or interest at risk too - bunkers he owns, containers and equipment he supplies, and freight or hire at risk - and so contributes in his own right. That exposure is insured under charterers' liability cover, and the allocation between owner and charterer is fixed by the general average clause of the charterparty, which typically incorporates the York-Antwerp Rules and may adjust allowances for wages, provisions and stores for periods when the ship is on hire.

Conclusion. A clause in a policy or charterparty dealing with the charterer's contribution is a contractual allocation of that general average exposure, read against the statutory doctrine of contribution - not a section of the Marine Insurance Act.

Four notes at four marks each means four equal answers, and the commonest failure is to write two pages on warranties, which every candidate knows, and three lines on the two that decide the grade. Budget the time by the marks. Within each note the reliable shape is definition - legal effect - practical relevance, which is exactly what a short note is for; a definition alone is worth about one mark of four.

blocks.h: The move that separates a strong answer here

blocks.p: Two of these four are in the Act and two are not, and saying so is worth marks rather than costing them. Deviation and warranties are statutory doctrines with sections behind them. A war risk clause is a policy wording, and a charterers' contribution clause is a charterparty or policy provision. The examiner has written 'As per the Marine Insurance Act' across all four, and the honest, high-scoring response is to answer each on its own footing and to say which footing that is - not to invent a section number so that all four look statutory.

The insurance excuses for deviation are narrower than the carriage ones. Carriage law protects a reasonable deviation, expressly including deviation to save property at sea. The Act's excuses stop at human life, or aiding a ship in distress where human life may be in danger. So a master who deviates to salvage an abandoned but valuable vessel may be perfectly safe against the cargo interest and may still have discharged the underwriter. Two regimes, two tests, one voyage - and the fact that the insurer's discharge runs from the time of deviation and is not cured by regaining the route is what makes it bite.

blocks.h: Why the warranty rule feels back to front

blocks.p: In ordinary contract law a warranty is the minor term: breach sounds in damages and the contract lives. In marine insurance the warranty is the severe term: it must be complied with exactly, materiality is irrelevant, and breach discharges the insurer from the date of breach. That inversion is the trap. Note also that the two jurisdictions have diverged - English textbooks now describe suspension under the Insurance Act 2015, while the Indian position is still discharge. In an Indian examination, answer on the 1963 Act.

ul: Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906. The operative Indian statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Applying the English Insurance Act 2015 suspension rule to an Indian policy.
Saying deviation avoids the policy from the outset. It discharges the insurer from the time of deviation - losses before it are still covered.
Saying the ship is safe once she rejoins her route. Regaining the route does not cure the deviation.
Treating an intention to deviate as a deviation. There must be a deviation in fact.
Importing the carriage-law excuse of saving property into the insurance list. It is not there.
Saying a hull and machinery time policy carries an implied warranty of seaworthiness. It does not - but privity of the assured defeats a loss attributable to unseaworthiness.
Presenting the war risk clause as a section of the Act, or as something that grants cover in the ordinary policy. It is an exclusion, with the cover bought back separately.
Inventing a section number for a 'Charterers Contribution Clause'. There is none - and saying so, then explaining contribution and the charterer's general average exposure, is the answer.

blocks.p:
"Your ship diverts to tow a disabled but unmanned barge to safety. Any insurance consequence?" Potentially yes. Saving property is not among the Act's excuses; the excuses run to human life, or aiding a ship in distress where human life may be in danger. Under the carriage regime the same act may well be a reasonable deviation. Report it and let the underwriter be told at once.

"You breach the lay-up warranty by two days and nothing happens. Are you covered afterwards?" Under the Indian Act, no - the insurer is discharged from the date of the breach and the position is not cured by the breach ending, unless the insurer waives it. Under English law since 2015 the answer would be different.

"Who pays if two policies cover the same loss?" The assured may claim under either but cannot recover more than the indemnity; as between the insurers they contribute rateably, and one who overpays has a right of contribution against the others.

ul: From what moment is the insurer discharged by a deviation? From the time of the deviation; it is immaterial that the ship regained her route before any loss.

Name three excuses for deviation. Authorised by a term of the policy; reasonably necessary for the safety of the ship or subject-matter; for saving human life or aiding a ship in distress where human life may be in danger.
Must a warranty be material to the risk? No - it must be exactly complied with whether it is material or not.
Give an express warranty in an H&M policy. A classification warranty, navigation or trading limits, or a lay-up warranty.
Is there an implied warranty of seaworthiness in a time policy? No, but privity of the assured defeats a loss attributable to unseaworthiness.

Which perils does the ordinary hull policy exclude and where are they bought back? War, capture, seizure, arrest, restraint, detainment, mines, terrorism and malicious acts - bought back under war risk hull and P&I cover.
Why does a charterer contribute in general average? Because he has property or interest at risk in the adventure - his bunkers, his equipment, and freight or hire at risk.

blocks.p: For every note: DEFINE - EFFECT - PRACTICE. Across the four: two in the Act, two in the policy - deviation and warranties are statute, war risks and charterers' contribution are contract. For deviation: from the time of deviation, and rejoining does not cure it. For warranties: exact compliance, materiality irrelevant, discharge from the date of breach.

ul: Marine Insurance Act, 1963 (India) - deviation and the excuses for deviation or delay; warranties at sections 35 to 43, including nature, exact compliance, when breach is excused, express warranties and the implied warranties of seaworthiness and legality; maritime perils at section 3; double insurance and the right of contribution; general average loss at section 66.
Insurance Act 2015 (United Kingdom) - changed the English consequence of breach of warranty to suspension. Not applicable in India.
Institute Time Clauses Hulls, International Hull Clauses, Institute War and Strikes Clauses, war risk P&I - named by identity only; no clause quoted, no edition asserted.
York-Antwerp Rules - contractual, applying only where the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them; Rule A defines the general average act.
The charterparty's own general average clause - where the charterer's contribution is actually allocated.

blocks.p: Three limits are declared. First, section numbers: the numbers given here for deviation, for the excuses and for the warranty provisions are taken from reproductions of the bare Act and from the Act's own scheme rather than from a certified statutory text, so quote the substance with confidence and the number with care - the doctrines are not in doubt, the numbering is what carries the risk. Second, the war risk wordings are commercial market documents rather than published law; the exclusion, the buy-back, the listed-area mechanism, the short-notice cancellation and the automatic termination triggers are described structurally, and no rate, no area and no clause number is asserted. Third, the absence of a 'Charterers Contribution Clause' from the Act is a finding, stated plainly in the answer rather than papered over with an invented citation - and stating it is worth more marks than inventing one.

questions.understand_first: Four labels are put in front of you under one heading, and the quiet test is whether you know that they do not all belong to the same thing. Two of them are rules the law imposes on the bargain, whatever the parties write. The first is about staying on the road you said you would take: if the ship wanders off the route the cover was priced for, the insurer stops being on risk from the moment she wanders, and it does not help that she found her way back before anything went wrong. There is a short list of good reasons for wandering, and it is narrower than most people expect - saving people counts, saving valuable property does not. The second is about promises you make about the ship that are treated as absolute. In ordinary contracts a promise like this is a minor term; here it is the harshest one on the page, because it has to be kept to the letter, it makes no difference whether keeping it would have mattered to the accident, and breaking it ends the cover from the moment it is broken rather than merely reducing what you can claim. The other two labels are not rules at all - they are pieces of the contract that the market writes. One of them exists to say what the ordinary policy will not pay for, so that dangerous political risks can be priced separately and switched off at short notice when the world changes. The last is about a simple fairness idea: when several parties all benefit from something that cost one of them, they share the bill in proportion to what they had at stake - and a charterer is one of those parties, because the fuel in the tanks and the money he stands to make are just as much at risk as the ship and the boxes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does a ship deviate, and what is the effect of an unexcused deviation?
retrieval_cards.answer: She deviates when she departs from the course specifically designated by the policy or, where none is designated, from the usual and customary course. Without lawful excuse the insurer is discharged from liability as from the time of deviation, and it is immaterial that she regained her route before any loss.
retrieval_cards.why: Intention to deviate is immaterial - there must be a deviation in fact.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is deviation to save property at sea excused under the Marine Insurance Act?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Act's excuses run to saving human life, or aiding a ship in distress where human life may be in danger. Saving property alone is not among them - although carriage law does protect a reasonable deviation to save property.
retrieval_cards.why: Two regimes, two tests: a master can be safe under the bill of lading and have prejudiced the policy.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the effect of breach of warranty under the Indian Marine Insurance Act, 1963?
retrieval_cards.answer: The warranty must be exactly complied with whether or not it is material to the risk, and on breach the insurer is discharged from liability as from the date of the breach, without prejudice to liability incurred before it, subject to express provision in the policy.
retrieval_cards.why: English law diverged under the Insurance Act 2015, where breach suspends rather than discharges.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Express and implied warranties - give an example of each in a hull and machinery policy.
retrieval_cards.answer: Express: a classification warranty, navigation or trading limits, or a lay-up warranty - written into or upon the policy. Implied: seaworthiness at the commencement of the voyage in a voyage policy, and legality of the adventure. A time policy carries no implied seaworthiness warranty, but privity of the assured defeats a loss attributable to unseaworthiness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the ordinary hull policy cover war risks?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - it excludes war, civil war, revolution, capture, seizure, arrest, restraint and detainment, derelict mines and torpedoes, terrorism and malicious acts. The cover is bought back separately under war risk hull, cargo and P&I wordings.
retrieval_cards.why: The war risk clause defines what the ordinary policy will not pay for; it is a policy clause, not a section of the Act.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does war risk cover operate commercially?
retrieval_cards.answer: Listed areas are designated by the market's war risk committee and attract an additional premium; the assured notifies entry into and departure from them; the cover is cancellable at short notice by either party; and it terminates automatically on the outbreak of war between the major powers or the hostile detonation of a nuclear weapon.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does 'contribution' mean in the Marine Insurance Act?
retrieval_cards.answer: The double insurance doctrine. Where the assured is over-insured because the same risk is covered more than once, he may claim under any policy but cannot recover more than the indemnity, and as between the insurers each contributes rateably in proportion to the amount for which he is liable, with a right of contribution against the others for an insurer who overpays.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does a 'Charterers Contribution Clause' come from, and why does a charterer contribute at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not from the Marine Insurance Act, which contains no clause of that name. It is a contractual provision in a policy or charterparty. A charterer contributes in general average because he has property or interest at risk in the adventure - bunkers he owns, containers and equipment he supplies, and freight or hire at risk - insured under charterers' liability cover and allocated by the charterparty's general average clause.
retrieval_cards.why: Attributing a contractual clause to a statutory section is the error the question is set to catch.
