blocks.h: (a) The reasons which could have led to this failure
1. What the stated condition tells you before any test is made

blocks.p: The question supplies one decisive fact: main electrical power remained intact. That rules out a blackout and everything downstream of it - no loss of the lubricating oil, cooling water, fuel booster or servo pumps through loss of supply, and no loss of the control and alarm system. The engine therefore stopped for a reason on its own side, and the causes divide into four families. It also means the ship is far better placed than she looks: steering gear, machinery, radio, lighting and the fire pumps are all still live.

ul: Loss of fuel supply pressure - booster pump failure, suction loss, or a service tank run down or drawn dry.
Filter blockage or a rapid differential-pressure rise, often after a fuel change or after heavy rolling has disturbed tank sediment.
Water, sludge or cat fines slug reaching the engine; a fuel of the wrong viscosity or a changeover error causing seizure of fuel pump plungers or injector needles.
Loss of heating or of viscosity control on a heavy fuel, stalling injection.
Air lock in the fuel system, or a leaking or vented high-pressure line.

blocks.p: This family is the most likely single explanation for a sudden stop with power intact, and it splits three ways - the engine has lost its control signal, the protective system has stopped it deliberately, or the governing system has failed.

ul: An automatic shutdown has operated on a genuine parameter - low lubricating oil pressure, high jacket or piston cooling outlet temperature, high thrust or main bearing temperature, oil mist detector alarm, or overspeed. The engine has protected itself and the trip is information, not a nuisance.
A spurious shutdown from a failed sensor, transmitter, wiring fault or a loss of the safety-system supply.
Loss of remote control from the bridge or engine control room - telegraph, remote control system, or the interface between them.
Governor or actuator failure, or loss of the governor's speed pick-up signal, taking fuel to zero.
Loss of control or starting air, or a control-air pressure low trip - even with generators running, an air compressor fault or a leak drops the control air that the whole system needs.

blocks.h: 4. Lubrication, cooling, mechanical and transmission causes

ul: Loss of lubricating oil pressure from a pump, filter, suction or sump problem - which will also have commanded the shutdown above.
Loss of cooling - sea water suction blocked or lost, central cooler, jacket circulating pump, or expansion tank level.
Mechanical seizure or damage - piston or bearing seizure, crankshaft or coupling damage, broken fuel cam or camshaft drive, turbocharger seizure or surge severe enough to stall the engine.

Transmission causes where fitted - controllable-pitch propeller hydraulic failure with the pitch running to zero, clutch or gearbox failure, or shaft, coupling or propeller damage such as a rope or net around the propeller.

blocks.h: 5. The first minutes - tell the bridge, then stabilise the plant

blocks.p: Inform the bridge immediately - before diagnosis, not after it. The Master must know at once that he has lost propulsion so that he can assess traffic and sea room, exhibit the lights or shapes for a vessel not under command, sound the appropriate signal, warn shipping and consider a navigational warning. Then, in the engine room: confirm steering gear is available and put both power units on; confirm the second generator is running or on standby so that a blackout cannot follow the propulsion failure; start standby lubricating oil, cooling and fuel pumps; start the air compressors and build control and starting air; and prepare the emergency generator for use. Log the time.

Read the alarm and shutdown record before touching a reset. The order in which alarms arrived usually names the cause, and resetting first destroys that evidence. Then work the four families in order of speed: control air and control position; the shutdown and slowdown channel that operated; lubricating oil pressure and sump level; cooling temperatures and flows; fuel supply pressure, filter differentials, temperature and viscosity. Turn the engine on the turning gear with indicator cocks open and look for water, oil or fuel; feel for local overheating; check crankcase and scavenge spaces once the engine is proved cool and safe to open, and check the shaft is free.

Do not attempt repeated blind restarts against an unexplained protective shutdown. A trip that fired for a real reason - low lubricating oil pressure, high bearing temperature, oil mist - will destroy the engine if it is reset and run. Restart only when the cause is identified and cleared, or when the trip has been positively proved spurious. Then start with the Master's permission, run at reduced load with the engine watched locally, take temperatures and pressures, and increase load progressively. Inform the Company and the DPA, record everything for the technical superintendent and class, and consider whether the defect must be reported.

blocks.h: 7. What changes - the ship is now in danger, not merely inconvenienced

blocks.p: Everything in (b)(i) still applies, and it applies faster. What is new is that a ship without propulsion in heavy weather loses steerage way and falls beam-on to the sea and swell. From that follow synchronous and heavy rolling with a real risk of cargo shift and of exceeding design accelerations; green water, deck damage and downflooding through vents and openings; slamming and structural loading; and, if there is a lee shore or an offshore installation downwind, a drift towards grounding with a calculable time to run. The engine room itself is now at risk: rolling causes loss of pump suction, sump and tank surging, boiler flame failure and filter disturbance, so a blackout can follow the propulsion failure even though power is presently intact.

ul: Give the Master a realistic estimate, and update it. His decisions - to call for a tug, to broadcast, to anchor, to prepare for abandonment - all turn on how long you will be. An optimistic figure is worse than no figure.

Help him hold the head. Use the rudder while steerage way remains; use the bow thruster if fitted; consider a sea anchor or drogue if carried; and use ballast and trim to lower the centre of gravity, minimise free surface, improve the roll period and keep the propeller and rudder immersed.

Secure the engine room for rolling before working in it. Lash gear and stores; forbid work at height and under suspended loads; watch sump, tank and header levels and change over suctions before they are lost; keep standby pumps running rather than on standby; and keep the boiler and generators under close watch.

Protect the electrical supply. Put a second generator on load and keep the third available; prepare and test the emergency generator; prepare emergency steering and man the steering flat; and confirm emergency lighting and the fire pumps.

Get help early rather than late. Recommend to the Master that a tug be requested while there is still sea room - a tug ordered in the first hour arrives while it can still help. Prepare the emergency towing arrangement, rig the towing pennant and brief the crew forward, and consider anchoring only if depth, holding ground and the Master's judgement allow.

Communications are the Master's. An urgency (PAN PAN) broadcast warns shipping and calls assistance for a disabled ship; a distress (MAYDAY) is made when the ship is in grave and imminent danger - which a lee shore, a failing hull or a shifted cargo can create quickly. I supply the technical facts; the Master transmits.

Restraint on the engine. The temptation to force a restart is strongest here and the consequence is worst here. A restart that seizes the engine removes the last chance of self-help, so the same rule holds: establish the cause, or prove the trip spurious, before turning. If partial power is achievable, even slow ahead is decisive - it restores steerage, lets the ship head into the sea and stops the drift.

Prepare for the worst case in parallel - watertight integrity confirmed, pollution prevention and SOPEP material ready, the Company and DPA informed under the emergency procedure, and the crew briefed.

blocks.p: The examiner has done the candidate a favour by writing 5 / 5 / 6 on the paper, and most candidates ignore it. Heavy weather carries more marks than calm weather, which can only mean that the heavy-weather answer must contain something the calm-weather answer does not. Write the calm-weather response in full, then write the heavy-weather response as what changes and what is added - the loss of steerage, the beam-on roll, the drift, the risk to the engine room itself, the tug, the urgency broadcast. Repeating the calm list with the word 'heavy' in front of it forfeits the extra mark and the examiner's goodwill.

blocks.h: The clue in the question that most answers walk past

blocks.p: 'With the main electrical power, however, remaining intact.' The word however is the examiner telling you this matters. It removes blackout from the cause list, and with it every consequential loss of pumps and control supply, so the cause lies on the engine's own side. It also tells you what you still have: steering gear, standby pumps, compressors, radio, lighting and fire pumps. An answer that starts by saying what the stated condition rules in and out is answering 'explain systematically'; an answer that lists thirty possible faults is not.

blocks.h: Trip, slowdown, and the discipline that separates a professional answer

blocks.p: A modern propulsion plant will slow itself down or stop itself to prevent damage. The parameters differ by installation - the ship's own trip schedule is the authority - but the principle does not: a shutdown is a diagnosis the engine has already made. Two consequences follow. First, read the alarm sequence before you reset anything, because the reset destroys the order of arrival, which is usually the whole diagnosis. Second, never crank against an unexplained shutdown. Low lubricating oil pressure, high bearing temperature and an oil mist alarm all mean that restarting turns a stoppage into a wrecked engine - and in heavy weather that removes the ship's last chance of saving herself. Saying this explicitly is worth marks; it is the single most common unsafe answer in this family.

blocks.h: Why beam-on is the whole of the heavy-weather problem

blocks.p: A ship keeps her head to the sea by going forward. Take the propulsion away and she loses steerage way, pays off, and settles beam-on to the sea and swell - the worst possible attitude. Rolling can become synchronous, accelerations rise, cargo and stores can shift, water comes on deck and can find vents and openings, and the ship begins to drift downwind at a rate that can be measured against the chart. This is why the heavy-weather answer is about heading, stability and time, and why any propulsion - even dead slow ahead - is transformative: it restores steerage, lets the ship head up, and stops the drift.

ul: Listing a blackout among the causes. The question says main power is intact.
Ignoring the 5 / 5 / 6 split and writing one undifferentiated response.
Resetting the trip first and reading the alarm log afterwards.
Recommending repeated restart attempts to 'see if it goes'. This is unsafe and is marked as such.
Forgetting to tell the bridge first. The Master cannot exhibit not-under-command signals or warn shipping if nobody tells him.
Treating not under command as something the engineer declares. The Master does, on your information.
Broadcasting distress from the engine room. Urgency and distress are transmitted on the Master's authority.
Leaving the ballast and stability limb out of the heavy-weather answer - it is the only lever the engine room shares with the bridge while the engine is dead.
Waiting to see whether the engine can be fixed before recommending a tug. Sea room is spent while you wait.
Forgetting that heavy rolling can blackout a ship whose power is currently intact, through lost suctions, surging sumps and boiler flame failure.

blocks.p:
"The shutdown was on low lubricating oil pressure but the pressure now reads normal. Do you start?" Not until you know why it fell. A momentary loss from a lost suction, a partly blocked filter or a surging sump in a seaway leaves normal pressure behind it and a damaged bearing ahead of it. Turn on the turning gear, check the sump, prove the pump and filter, and take bearing temperatures on restart.

"You are drifting towards a lee shore and can give slow ahead only. Do you use it?" Yes, and tell the Master at once. Steerage way is worth more than power - it lets him head up and stops the drift - and partial power ordered early beats full power promised later.

"Who declares not under command?" The Master. Your duty is to tell him immediately and honestly what you have and how long you need.

ul: What does 'main electrical power intact' rule out? A blackout, and every loss of pumps, control supply and alarm system that follows from one.
What do you read before resetting? The alarm and shutdown record, in order of arrival.

Name three parameters that commonly command a shutdown. Low lubricating oil pressure, high jacket or piston cooling outlet temperature, and oil mist detection or overspeed - but the ship's own trip schedule governs.

What is the difference between a slowdown and a shutdown? A slowdown reduces load to protect the engine while leaving the ship some propulsion; a shutdown stops it. Both are diagnoses the safety system has already made.

What can a disabled ship do about her heading? Rudder while way remains, bow thruster if fitted, sea anchor or drogue if carried, and ballast and trim to manage rolling and keep rudder and propeller immersed.

When is it PAN PAN and when is it MAYDAY? Urgency for a disabled ship needing assistance without grave and imminent danger; distress when there is grave and imminent danger. Both on the Master's authority.
Why request a tug early? Because sea room, not engineering optimism, is what decides whether a tug can still help when she arrives.

blocks.p: For the causes, four families: FUEL - CONTROL - LUBE AND COOL - MECHANICAL (steps 2 to 4), sitting under one gate - power is intact, so the fault is on the engine's side. For the response: TELL - STABILISE - READ - DECIDE in calm weather; and in heavy weather add HEAD - STABILITY - SURVIVE - HELP. One sentence carries the safety rule in both: never crank against a trip you cannot explain.

ul: COLREGs 1972 - a vessel not under command through some exceptional circumstance, and the lights, shapes and sound signal for one. Exhibited by the Master on the engineer's information.

SOLAS chapter V - the Master's discretion for safe navigation and the obligation to broadcast danger messages. SOLAS chapter IV / GMDSS - urgency (PAN PAN) and distress (MAYDAY), on the Master's authority.
ISM Code Part A element 5 - the Master's responsibility and overriding authority; element 8 - emergency preparedness, procedures and drills. The Code has elements and paragraphs, not regulations.
SOLAS chapter II-1 - the emergency source of electrical power, and emergency steering arrangements. Cited by concept for the standby-capability limb; no regulation number asserted.
The engine's trip and slowdown schedule is the maker's and the ship's own document, and it - not a textbook list - is the authority for which parameter does what.
No instrument prescribes a fault list or a heavy-weather response; both are declared as engineering and seamanship practice.

blocks.p: Two limits are declared rather than hidden. The trip schedule is installation-specific: which parameters command a slowdown, which command a shutdown, and whether either may be overridden are set by the engine builder's safety system and the ship's approved arrangement, so the answer states the principle and sends the candidate to the ship's own schedule instead of asserting a universal list. Equipment is ship-specific: bow thruster, controllable-pitch propeller, shaft generator, sea anchor and emergency towing arrangement are each conditioned on the ship being so fitted. The cause families and the response sequence are declared as engineering and seamanship practice, because no instrument prescribes either.

steps.title: Diagnosis, and the restart decision
points: read the alarm and shutdown record before touching a reset
work control air, trip channel, lube oil, cooling and fuel in that order
turn on the turning gear with indicator cocks open; check crankcase when safe
no repeated blind restarts against an unexplained shutdown

reduced load, watched locally, load increased progressively
inform the Company and the DPA and record everything

steps.title: What changes - the ship is now in danger, not merely inconvenienced

heavy and possibly synchronous rolling, cargo shift, green water and downflooding
slamming and structural loading

steps.title: The heavy-weather actions
points: give the Master a realistic estimate and keep updating it
help hold the head - rudder while way remains, bow thruster, sea anchor, ballast and trim

questions.understand_first: One sentence in the question does most of the work, and it is the one that looks like a throwaway: the lights are still on. If the ship had gone dark, everything would follow from that - no pumps, no cooling, no control - and the engine stopping would be a symptom rather than the problem. Because the power stayed up, all of those services were there when the engine stopped, so whatever went wrong went wrong inside the propulsion system itself. That single deduction turns an unmanageable list of possibilities into four manageable groups: it did not get fuel, it was not told to run or was told to stop, it lost the oil or the cooling it needs to survive, or something inside it broke or jammed. The other idea worth holding is about the third of those. A modern engine watches itself and will stop itself rather than be destroyed - so when it stops on its own, it has already made a diagnosis, and the record of which alarm came first is that diagnosis written down. Wiping it out by pressing reset, and then cranking to see what happens, is how a stoppage becomes a wreck. Finally, the weather changes the problem completely, and not in the way of making it merely more unpleasant. A ship keeps her nose into the sea by moving forward. Stop her and she slews round until the sea is hitting her on the side, which is the one attitude everything aboard is least designed for - and meanwhile the wind is quietly carrying her somewhere, and somewhere may have rocks in it. So in bad weather the question stops being 'what broke' and becomes 'which way is she pointing, how long have I got, and who is coming'.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does 'main electrical power remaining intact' rule out, and what does it leave you?
retrieval_cards.answer: It rules out a blackout and every consequential loss - pumps, control supply, alarm system - so the fault lies on the engine's own side. It leaves steering gear, standby pumps, compressors, radio, lighting and fire pumps all available.
retrieval_cards.why: The deduction is what turns an open-ended fault list into four families.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the four families of cause for a sudden stop at full ahead with power intact.
retrieval_cards.answer: Fuel; control, automation and the protective system; lubrication and cooling; and mechanical or transmission failure. The control family is the most likely single explanation and splits three ways - lost control signal, deliberate protective shutdown, or governor failure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The engine has tripped and you do not know why. Do you reset and restart?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Read the alarm and shutdown record in order of arrival first - the reset destroys it. Restart only when the cause is identified and cleared, or the trip has been positively proved spurious, and then with the Master's permission at reduced load under local watch.
retrieval_cards.why: A trip on low lube oil pressure, high bearing temperature or oil mist will destroy the engine if it is reset and run.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are your first actions in the engine room, in calm weather?
retrieval_cards.answer: Inform the bridge immediately, before diagnosis. Then confirm steering gear is available with both power units on; put a second generator on load or standby so a blackout cannot follow; start standby lubricating oil, cooling and fuel pumps; build control and starting air; prepare the emergency generator; and log the time.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a disabled ship in heavy weather go beam-on, and why does that matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Without propulsion she loses steerage way and pays off until the sea is on the beam. That brings heavy and possibly synchronous rolling, risk of cargo shift, green water and downflooding, slamming, and a measurable drift downwind towards any lee shore.
retrieval_cards.why: It is why even dead slow ahead is transformative - it restores steerage and stops the drift.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the engine room do that is specific to heavy weather?
retrieval_cards.answer: Give the Master a realistic and updated estimate; help hold the head with rudder, bow thruster, sea anchor and ballast or trim; secure the space against rolling and keep standby pumps running rather than on standby; watch sumps, headers and suctions for surging; prepare the emergency generator and emergency steering; and recommend a tug early while sea room remains.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who declares not under command, and who transmits urgency or distress?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Master, in both cases. Not under command is a COLREGs status shown by lights, shapes and sound signal; urgency (PAN PAN) and distress (MAYDAY) are transmitted on the Master's authority under the GMDSS. The Chief Engineer's duty is to give him the technical facts immediately and honestly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can a ship with power intact still black out in heavy weather?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Rolling causes loss of pump suction, surging sumps and tanks, filter disturbance and boiler flame failure, so a blackout can follow the propulsion failure. That is why a second generator goes on load and the emergency generator is prepared rather than assumed.

blocks.h: 1. The limit, and the equivalence that makes a scrubber lawful

blocks.p:
The primary driver is MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14, which caps the sulphur content of fuel oil used on board - 0.50 per cent m/m globally, and 0.10 per cent m/m inside an Emission Control Area. Regulation 14 controls the fuel, and on its face it would force every ship onto distillate or low-sulphur residual fuel.

What makes a scrubber possible is a second provision. Regulation 4 - Equivalents allows the Administration to accept a fitting or method as an alternative to a requirement of the Annex if it is at least as effective in terms of emission reductions. An exhaust gas cleaning system is approved under regulation 4 as an equivalent means of compliance: the ship may burn high-sulphur fuel provided the emissions meet the ratio corresponding to the applicable fuel limit, verified against the 2021 EGCS Guidelines, resolution MEPC.340(77), and evidenced by the approval documentation, the onboard monitoring manual and the continuous monitoring record.

So the correct one-line answer is: compliance with the regulation 14 sulphur limits, achieved by an equivalent method permitted under regulation 4, rather than by buying compliant fuel. The commercial driver behind the regulatory one is the price spread between high-sulphur and compliant fuel, which is what makes the capital investment worth making.

blocks.h: (b) HSFO and an open-loop scrubber entering a zero-discharge zone
2. The constraint the scenario imposes, before any action

blocks.p:
Two things must be established first. An open-loop system cannot be turned into a closed-loop system. Only a hybrid unit can change mode, and only if it was built and approved with the alkali dosing plant, process tank, holding tank and cooling that closed-loop operation needs. If the ship truly has an open-loop scrubber, there is no operating mode that lets her keep burning HSFO in a zone where the discharge is prohibited.

Second, the zone is a matter of local law, not of MARPOL. At this date there is no global IMO prohibition on discharge water from exhaust gas cleaning systems; the international work is still in progress. What exists is a growing patchwork of national, port and regional restrictions, which differ from one another - some ban open-loop discharge only, some ban all EGCS discharge, some restrict the fuel as well. The port's own published requirement is the controlling document, obtained through the agent and the Company before arrival.

blocks.h: 3. The operational switch - planning and timing

blocks.p: The switch is a changeover to compliant low-sulphur fuel with the scrubber discharge stopped, and it must be complete before the ship crosses into the zone. Working backwards from the entry position:

ul: Establish the applicable limit for the zone - 0.50 per cent, or 0.10 per cent if it is also an ECA - and confirm which grades on board meet it.

Calculate the changeover time from the volume held in the service and settling tanks, the piping and the heaters, and the consumption rate. The system does not flush instantly; residual high-sulphur fuel persists long after the valve is changed.
Start early enough that the changeover is finished at the boundary, and follow the ship's written changeover procedure, which MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14.6 requires her to carry.
Brief the watchkeepers and the bridge, and agree the entry time and position with the Master.

blocks.h: 4. The operational switch - engines, boilers, tanks and the unit itself

ul: Tank segregation and compatibility. Use segregated tanks and avoid commingling HSFO and VLSFO, which can be unstable together and drop asphaltenic sludge; keep the retained bunker samples and the analysis results to hand.

Temperature and viscosity. Cool the fuel gradually to the required viscosity at the injector - a rapid temperature change is what seizes fuel pump plungers and injector needles and can stop the main engine. Respect the maker's rate-of-change limit.

Main and auxiliary engines. Change over together where they share the service system, watch fuel pump and injector behaviour, and adjust the cylinder oil feed rate and base number to the lower sulphur content.

Boilers. The question is explicit that the switch covers boilers too: change over the auxiliary and composite boiler burners, re-set burner atomising temperature and check the flame, since a low-viscosity fuel behaves differently and flame failure is a real risk during the change.

The scrubber itself. Stop the discharge. Bypass the tower or run it dry in accordance with the maker's instructions, close the overboard, secure the wash water pumps, and be careful of exhaust temperature and back pressure in the bypassed condition. If, and only if, the unit is a hybrid, closed-loop mode with the bleed-off retained in the holding tank is the alternative - subject to holding-tank capacity and to the zone permitting closed-loop discharge at all.
Residues. EGCS residue is never discharged to sea; it is retained and landed to a port reception facility, with the receipt kept.

blocks.p: The switch is proved by paper. Record, as regulation 14.6 requires, the volume of low-sulphur fuel oil in each tank and the date, time and position of the ship when the changeover was completed prior to entry - and again when it is commenced prior to exit. Keep the EGCS monitoring record and the record book, the bunker delivery notes and the sealed samples, the port reception facility receipt for residues, and the entry in the engine room log. Port State control will read these before it looks at any machinery.

blocks.h: 6. The compliance risks of failing to transition

ul: Breach of the port or coastal State's own law - the immediate risk. Discharge in a prohibited zone attracts detention, fines on the company and often on the Master personally, and in some jurisdictions criminal liability.

Breach of MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 itself if the ship instead keeps burning HSFO with the scrubber shut down. The equivalence under regulation 4 is only good while the equivalent is operating; a bypassed scrubber and high-sulphur fuel is simply non-compliant fuel.
Evidential failure. A gap in the continuous monitoring record, or a record that does not match the passage, is treated as seriously as the discharge - and a falsified record far more seriously.
Port State control detention and delay, with the deficiency recorded against the ship and the company on the regional inspection database.

Commercial consequences - off-hire, delay and demurrage, breach of the charterparty's compliance warranties, refusal of future port entry, and loss of standing with charterers who audit environmental performance.
Insurance consequences. A deliberate breach of a discharge restriction is not the same risk as an accident, and P&I cover responds differently to a knowing violation.
Safety consequence. A rushed or late changeover carries its own risk of loss of propulsion at exactly the moment the ship is entering confined water.

blocks.h: 7. The economic trade-off - VLSFO against a scrubber

blocks.p: The scrubber case is a single arithmetic proposition: the annual saving equals the HSFO-to-VLSFO price spread multiplied by annual fuel consumption, and it must exceed the annualised capital cost plus the operating cost. The variables on each side are what the discussion is about.

rows: Capital
High. The unit, funnel and casing modification, pumps, piping, tanks and monitoring equipment - plus off-hire and yard time for the retrofit, which is often the larger number.
None. This is the whole of its commercial attraction.
Running cost

A parasitic electrical load for the wash water pumps, which raises fuel consumption; maintenance of an aggressive corrosive duty; monitoring instrument calibration; residue landing fees; alkali consumption in closed or hybrid mode; extra crew workload and training; and additional survey and class scope.
The fuel price premium over HSFO, and nothing else.
Technical risk
Downtime of the unit means immediate loss of compliance, so a defect is a commercial as well as a technical event.
Blend instability and incompatibility, cat fines, low viscosity and lubricity, cold flow and wax, and cylinder oil base number matching.
Regulatory risk

The decisive one. Every new local discharge restriction shrinks the area in which the investment earns, and the ship must carry compliant fuel and segregated tankage for those areas anyway - so she pays part of both bills.
Low. Compliant fuel is accepted everywhere the limit applies.

blocks.p: Two points close the discussion honestly. First, the spread is volatile and is not contracted: a payback calculated on a wide spread evaporates when the spread narrows, and no owner can hold it. Second, the regulatory envelope is narrowing rather than widening - the international work on EGCS discharge was still under development at this date, and in the North-East Atlantic a regional ban on open-loop discharges in internal waters and ports takes effect from 1 July 2027, with closed-loop discharges to follow from 1 January 2029. Both are in the future at present, but an investment appraisal made today has to price them. For a container ship on a fixed liner rotation the answer therefore depends less on the spread than on how much of her trading pattern lies inside restricted water - which is exactly why she is in this scenario carrying both a scrubber and compliant fuel.

Limb (a) is worth 4 and has a one-sentence answer; do not spend a page on the history of sulphur regulation. Limb (b) is worth 12 and contains three printed demands - the operational switch, the compliance risks, the economic trade-off - so budget roughly four marks to each and give each its own heading. The single highest-value sentence in the whole answer is the one that says an open-loop unit cannot become a closed-loop unit; most answers to this question quietly assume it can, and the whole of the rest of their operational limb is then fiction.

blocks.h: Regulation 14 sets the limit; regulation 4 lets you meet it another way

blocks.p: This pairing is the conceptual core of limb (a) and it is worth stating explicitly. Regulation 14 is written about the fuel - it caps the sulphur content of fuel oil used on board. Taken alone it would make a scrubber irrelevant, because a ship burning three per cent fuel breaches it however clean her funnel gas is. Regulation 4 is the door: it lets an Administration accept an alternative that is at least as effective in emission terms. The scrubber is that alternative, and everything else - the approval, the monitoring manual, the continuous record - exists to prove the equivalence is real and continuing. The corollary is the trap in limb (b): switch the equivalent off and keep burning the high-sulphur fuel, and you are straightforwardly in breach of regulation 14.

blocks.h: Where the zero-discharge rule actually comes from

blocks.p: It does not come from MARPOL. At this date there is no global IMO ban on EGCS discharge water - the international work was still in progress, with proposals invited to the pollution prevention sub-committee. What exists is local: national, port and regional restrictions, which differ in scope and change frequently. A candidate who says 'MARPOL prohibits open-loop discharge in ports' has made a real error. The correct statement is that MARPOL permits the equivalent, the 2021 EGCS Guidelines set the discharge water criteria and the monitoring, and the port decides whether it will accept the discharge at all. Know also that the direction of travel is one way: the North-East Atlantic regional ban bites on 1 July 2027 for open loop and 1 January 2029 for closed loop - both still ahead of this sitting, so state them as future.

blocks.h: Why the changeover is a propulsion-safety event, not just a paperwork event

blocks.p: Going from heavy fuel to a low-viscosity compliant fuel means cooling the fuel, and doing it too quickly is a classic cause of fuel pump plunger and injector needle seizure - which stops the main engine. The ship is by definition close to or entering port when this happens. So the changeover is planned backwards from the boundary with a calculated flushing time, executed at the maker's permitted rate of temperature change, and watched. The boiler limb matters for the same reason: burner atomising temperature and flame behaviour change with the fuel, and flame failure during a changeover is common. This is also where the question links to any propulsion-failure scenario - a botched changeover is one of the fuel-side causes of a sudden stop.

blocks.h: How to discuss economics without inventing numbers

blocks.p: The examiner asks for a discussion, not a spreadsheet, and quoting a fuel price or a payback period in an exam answer is a gift to a follow-up question you cannot win. State the proposition - saving equals spread times consumption, and must beat annualised capital plus operating cost - and then discuss the variables: the volatility of the spread, the off-hire cost of the retrofit, the parasitic load, the maintenance of a corrosive duty, residue landing, and above all the shrinking operating envelope as more water becomes restricted. That last point is the mature one, and it is the reason a ship in this scenario ends up paying for both solutions at once.

ul: Saying the crew simply switches the open-loop scrubber to closed loop. Only a hybrid unit can do that, and only if it was built and approved for it.
Saying MARPOL prohibits open-loop discharge in ports. It does not; the restriction is local or regional, and the international measure was still under development at this sitting.
Answering limb (a) with 'to reduce air pollution'. The driver is a specific limit - regulation 14 - met by a specific mechanism - the regulation 4 equivalent.
Bypassing the scrubber and continuing on HSFO. That is a breach of regulation 14, because the equivalence only holds while the equivalent is operating.
Starting the changeover at the boundary instead of finishing it there.
Cooling the fuel too fast and seizing fuel pumps on the approach.
Forgetting the boilers, which the question names expressly.
Forgetting the record: volume in each tank, and the date, time and position when the changeover was completed.
Discharging EGCS residue overboard. It is landed to a reception facility.
Quoting a fuel price, a spread or a payback period.
Treating the regional 2027 and 2029 bans as already in force. Both are future at this sitting.

blocks.p:
"Your scrubber fails at sea and you have only HSFO aboard. Are you compliant?" No. The regulation 4 equivalence holds only while the equivalent works. Inform the Administration and the port State, seek instructions, and consider a fuel oil non-availability report if compliant fuel genuinely could not be obtained - but a failed scrubber does not make high-sulphur fuel lawful.

"The port bans open-loop discharge but you have a hybrid unit. Problem solved?" Only if the port also accepts closed-loop discharge, and only within your holding-tank capacity for the time alongside. Some zones prohibit all EGCS discharge, in which case you are back to compliant fuel.

"Which is the greater risk to the investment - the fuel price or the regulator?" The regulator. A narrowed spread reduces the return; a restricted trading area removes it, and the direction of regulation has been one way.

ul: Which regulation caps the sulphur, and which permits the scrubber? Regulation 14 caps the fuel; regulation 4 permits an equivalent at least as effective in emission terms.
What are the two limits? 0.50 per cent m/m globally and 0.10 per cent m/m in an Emission Control Area.
Which resolution carries the EGCS Guidelines? MEPC.340(77), the 2021 Guidelines, effective 1 June 2022.
What must be recorded at a changeover? The volume of low-sulphur fuel in each tank, and the date, time and position when the changeover was completed prior to entry - and commenced prior to exit.
Where does EGCS residue go? To a port reception facility, with the receipt retained. Never overboard.
Can an open-loop unit run closed loop? No, unless it is a hybrid unit built and approved for both.
When does the North-East Atlantic regional ban take effect? Open-loop discharges in internal waters and ports from 1 July 2027, closed-loop from 1 January 2029 - both future at this sitting.

blocks.p: For (a): 14 SETS IT, 4 LETS YOU MEET IT ANOTHER WAY. For (b), three demands and one gate. The gate is OPEN LOOP CANNOT CLOSE. Then SWITCH - RISK - MONEY: switch is calculate, change over early, stop the discharge, record it; risk is local law, regulation 14, the record, the port State, the charterer, the insurer; money is spread times consumption against capital plus running cost, in a shrinking envelope.

questions.short_title: Scrubbers - Regulatory Driver, Zero-Discharge Zone and the Economics

quick_revision.recall_15s: Driver: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 caps fuel sulphur at 0.50 per cent globally and 0.10 per cent in an ECA; regulation 4 lets an Administration accept an equivalent at least as effective in emission terms, and the scrubber is that equivalent under the 2021 EGCS Guidelines, MEPC.340(77). Scenario: an OPEN-LOOP unit cannot become closed-loop - only a hybrid can - and the zero-discharge rule is LOCAL, not MARPOL. So the switch is a changeover to compliant fuel COMPLETED BEFORE the boundary, calculated from system volume, executed at the maker's rate of cooling, covering engines and boilers, with the discharge stopped, residues landed ashore and the tank volume, date, time and position recorded. Risks: local law, breach of regulation 14 if you bypass and stay on HSFO, monitoring-record gaps, detention, off-hire, charterparty and insurance. Economics: spread times consumption against annualised capital plus running cost, in a shrinking regulatory envelope.

questions.understand_first: The rule everyone remembers is about fuel: ships may only burn fuel below a certain sulphur content. But there is a second rule sitting behind it which says, in effect, we care about what comes out of the funnel, not about what goes into the tank - so if you can show that your exhaust is as clean as it would have been on the good fuel, you may burn the cheap fuel. A scrubber is the machine that makes that argument, by washing the sulphur out of the exhaust gas with seawater. Which immediately raises the question the whole second half turns on: where does that washing water go? In the simple version of the machine it goes straight back over the side, having done its job, and that is why the machine is cheap to run and why some ports do not want it anywhere near them. Now hold two facts together. The first is that a machine built to take water in and put it out again cannot be talked into keeping the water instead - that is a different, more expensive machine with tanks and chemicals, and you either bought it or you did not. The second is that the ban in the question is not the international rulebook talking; it is a particular harbour saying not here. Put those together and the situation resolves itself: this ship has exactly one lawful move, which is to stop making the argument and simply burn the expensive fuel while she is inside that boundary - and to have finished switching over before she crosses it, because a fuel changeover takes time and does not respect lines on a chart. Everything after that is about proving you did it, and about the harder commercial question of whether buying the machine was ever the better bet when the number of places that will accept it keeps falling.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which two regulations of MARPOL Annex VI make a scrubber both necessary and lawful?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 14 caps the sulphur content of fuel oil used on board - 0.50 per cent m/m globally and 0.10 per cent m/m in an Emission Control Area. Regulation 4 permits an Administration to accept an equivalent that is at least as effective in terms of emission reductions, and the exhaust gas cleaning system is that equivalent.
retrieval_cards.why: Regulation 14 is written about the fuel, so without regulation 4 a scrubber would be irrelevant.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can an open-loop scrubber be switched to closed-loop operation?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Only a hybrid unit built and approved with the alkali dosing plant, process and holding tanks and cooling can change mode. An open-loop-only ship entering a zone where discharge is prohibited must change over to compliant low-sulphur fuel.
retrieval_cards.why: Most answers to this scenario assume the switch is possible, and everything that follows from that assumption is wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does MARPOL prohibit open-loop discharge in ports?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not at this sitting. MARPOL permits the equivalent and the 2021 EGCS Guidelines set the discharge water criteria and monitoring; whether the discharge is accepted is decided by national, port and regional rules. The international measure was still under development.
retrieval_cards.why: The regional North-East Atlantic ban takes effect from 1 July 2027 for open loop and 1 January 2029 for closed loop - both future at this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You bypass the scrubber and stay on HSFO inside the zone. Are you compliant?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The regulation 4 equivalence holds only while the equivalent is actually operating. A bypassed scrubber with high-sulphur fuel in the engine is simply non-compliant fuel, and that is a breach of regulation 14 itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must be recorded for a fuel changeover?
retrieval_cards.answer: The volume of low-sulphur fuel oil in each tank, and the date, time and position of the ship when the changeover operation was completed prior to entry - and again when it was commenced prior to exit. Keep also the EGCS monitoring record, the bunker delivery notes and sealed samples, and the reception facility receipt for residues.
retrieval_cards.why: Port State control reads the records before it looks at any machinery.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a fuel changeover a propulsion-safety event?
retrieval_cards.answer: Going to a low-viscosity compliant fuel means cooling the fuel, and cooling it faster than the maker permits seizes fuel pump plungers and injector needles - stopping the main engine just as the ship enters confined water. Boiler burners must be changed and re-set too, and flame failure during a changeover is common.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the scrubber investment case in one proposition.
retrieval_cards.answer: The annual saving equals the HSFO-to-compliant-fuel price spread multiplied by annual consumption, and it must exceed the annualised capital cost plus the operating cost - the parasitic pumping load, corrosive-duty maintenance, monitoring calibration, residue landing, alkali and crew workload.
retrieval_cards.why: The spread is volatile and cannot be contracted, so the sensitivity, not the headline number, is the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the greater long-term risk to a scrubber investment - the fuel price or the regulator?
retrieval_cards.answer: The regulator. A narrowed price spread reduces the return, but a shrinking area in which discharge is permitted removes it - and a ship that must carry compliant fuel and segregated tankage for restricted water anyway ends up paying part of both bills.

blocks.h: (a) The five-step safety briefing before entry and cleaning

blocks.p: I would open by correcting the word in the question: the board is not dead because it is switched off. It is dead only when it has been proved dead, at the point of work, and only in the section we have isolated - the rest of a main switchboard is still supplying the ship.

blocks.h: 1. Isolate - and find every source of supply

blocks.p: Identify the exact section from the single-line diagram, not by eye. Open and rack out or withdraw the incoming breaker to the isolated position, and then hunt the supplies that do not come from where you expect: the other generators and the bus-tie, the shore supply, the emergency switchboard interconnector (which can back-feed), a shaft generator, transformer back-feed from the low-voltage side, and the separately fed control, heater, UPS and battery supplies inside the panel. Every one is listed on the isolation schedule and every one is opened.

blocks.h: 2. Lock off, tag and hold the key

blocks.p: Each isolation is locked in the open or withdrawn position and carries a danger notice naming the permit, the work and the person. There is one key and it stays with the permit holder - not in a drawer and not with the duty engineer. Only the person who applied a lock removes it. Shutters over the busbar spouts are locked, and the breaker is padlocked in the test or isolated position.

blocks.h: 3. Prove dead - and prove the instrument that proves it

blocks.p: Use an approved voltage detector rated for the system, and use it prove - test - prove: prove the detector on a known live source or an approved proving unit, test the conductors, then prove the detector again, so that a detector which failed during the test cannot mislead you. Test all phases to each other and every phase to earth, and test at the point of work. Never accept an indicator lamp, a panel voltmeter, a breaker position indicator or somebody's word as proof - lamps fail dark and that is precisely how people are killed.

blocks.h: 4. Earth, and discharge the stored energy

blocks.p: On a high-voltage board, apply the earthing switch or portable earths after proving dead, so that any inadvertent re-energisation trips rather than kills; earths are applied and removed only by the permit holder and are recorded. On any board, deal with stored energy: discharge and short power-factor correction capacitors and let them stand, discharge the d.c. link of any variable-frequency drive, isolate UPS and battery-backed control supplies which do not die with the busbar, and discharge the closing and tripping springs of a spring-charged breaker mechanism before putting hands near it.

blocks.h: 5. Control the space, the tools and the person

blocks.p: Screen or barrier every adjacent live section and mark the safe working limit, because the real hazard when cleaning a dead panel is the live one beside it. Wear arc-rated clothing, a face shield, insulating gloves and use an insulating mat; remove rings, watches and chains; use insulated tools and tally them in and out. Clean with a vacuum and lint-free cloths and an approved non-conductive cleaner - never water, and never compressed air, which drives conductive dust into the live section next door. Never work alone: a second competent person stands by, knows how to isolate, is trained in resuscitation, and the rescue hook and first-aid arrangements are to hand. Finally, I would ask him to tell me back what he is going to do - a briefing that is not repeated back has not been received.

blocks.h: (b) The Permit to Work under the Safety Management System

blocks.p: The permit is a controlled document of the Company's Safety Management System - required by the ISM Code, which obliges the Company to establish procedures for key shipboard operations concerning safety, and to ensure personnel are competent and properly familiarised. Issue runs as follows:

ul: A risk assessment or job safety analysis is completed first, and a toolbox talk held with everyone who will work.
The Chief Engineer - or the person the SMS authorises - issues the permit to a named competent recipient. Nobody issues a permit to himself.

The permit states the exact equipment and the limits of the work, the isolations made and listed on an isolation schedule, the precautions taken, the PPE required, what nearby remains live, and the period of validity.
The recipient signs to accept, confirming he has understood the precautions and inspected the isolations himself.
Copies are displayed at the work site and on the permit board in the engine control room, and the bridge and duty engineer are informed so nothing is started or changed over in ignorance.

blocks.p: Where high voltage is involved the control tightens. Systems generally taken under class rules as exceeding 1,000 V require a separate high-voltage permit; work is authorised only for a person appointed in writing as competent for high voltage; earthing is mandatory and is itself recorded; and testing that requires the earths off is governed by a distinct sanction-to-test document with its own sign-off. The permit is time-limited, lapses at the stated expiry or at a change of watch, must be re-validated or re-issued rather than allowed to run on, and is suspended immediately if conditions change.
Closing is the mirror image and is done in this order, not in any other:

ul: All persons withdrawn and accounted for by name.
Tools, test leads, rags and materials removed and tallied against what went in.
Temporary earths removed by the permit holder and the removal recorded.
Covers, shrouds, barriers and screens replaced and the enclosure secured.
The recipient signs the work complete and declares the equipment safe to re-energise.
The issuer signs the permit cancelled - and only then are locks and tags removed, each by the person who fitted it.

The permit is filed as an SMS record, the work entered in the planned maintenance system, and the permit reviewed in the safety committee or internal audit under the Company's own verification and review obligations.

blocks.p:
Mechanical and visual: everything reassembled to the maker's arrangement, no foreign object, tool tally reconciled, cable and busbar connections torqued to the specified value - a loose joint is the classic cause of a switchboard fire - covers and phase barriers refitted and labelling correct.

Electrical: take insulation resistance readings phase to phase and phase to earth at the correct test voltage, with electronics and surge devices disconnected, and compare against the previous recorded values rather than merely against a pass figure; confirm earth continuity and bonding of the enclosure; and check the earth fault monitoring is restored.

Protection: verify relay settings against the approved setting schedule and the discrimination study - a setting quietly changed during maintenance is a fault that only appears on the day of a real fault - and function-test the trips and interlocks: over-current and short-circuit, reverse power, under-voltage release, preferential trip or load shedding where fitted, breaker interlocks, and the automatic changeover to the emergency switchboard.
Restoration is done deliberately and with the ship informed:

ol: Confirm the permit is closed, all earths off, all locks and tags removed, and the space clear of people and tools.
Inform the bridge and the duty engineer, agree the timing against the ship's operational state, and log it.
Energise the busbar first with every outgoing breaker open. Check voltage, frequency, phase sequence and insulation monitoring, and confirm synchronising and load sharing between generators.
Close the outgoing feeders progressively, essential services first and the largest loads last, watching each for abnormal current, arcing sound, smell, smoke or vibration.
Take a thermographic or temperature check on the joints that were disturbed, once loaded.

Restore the emergency switchboard interconnector and prove the emergency arrangements that were affected - emergency generator auto-start on loss of main power, emergency lighting, steering gear on both power units, and the fire pumps.

Update the planned maintenance system with the test results and readings, inform the Company, and where the work touched a class item, arrange the surveyor's attendance before the equipment is credited.

blocks.p: Only when all of that is done, and the readings are recorded, do I declare the main switchboard fully operational.

Three limbs at 5 / 6 / 5, and limb (a) comes with its own instruction: five steps. Give five, number them, and do not give four or seven - the examiner has told you the shape of the answer he wants and matching it is free marks. Limb (b) is the largest at 6 and has two halves - issuing and closing - plus a rider about high voltage; answer all three or lose a third of the limb. Limb (c) is a sequence question, so write it as a sequence.

blocks.h: The idea the whole question is built on

blocks.p: 'Dead' is a conclusion you reach, not a condition you assume. A switch in the off position, a lamp that is not lit, a breaker showing 'open' - none of these is evidence. The only evidence is a test with an instrument that you have proved works, at the point where the hands will go, immediately before the hands go there. Everything else in limb (a) - the isolation hunt, the locks, the earths, the screens - exists either to make that conclusion true or to keep it true while the work goes on. If you write one sentence of judgement in this question, write that one.

blocks.h: The hazard that is actually going to hurt him

blocks.p: Not the panel he is cleaning. The one next to it. A ship cannot black herself out to clean one switchboard section, so the section is isolated while the board either side of it carries the ship's entire load. That single fact drives half of limb (a): screen the adjacent sections, mark the safe working limit, insulated tools, tally them, no jewellery, and no compressed air - because blowing dust out of a dead panel deposits a conductive cloud into a live one. It is also why he never works alone, and why the standby man must know how to isolate and be able to resuscitate.

blocks.h: Prove - test - prove, in one line

blocks.p: Prove the detector on a known live source or proving unit; test the conductors; prove the detector again. The last step is the one candidates omit and it is the only one that catches the failure mode that kills - an indicator that failed between the first proof and the test, and therefore reads dead on live conductors. Test all phases and every phase to earth, because a single-phase test can miss a back-feed.

Opening the breaker does not empty the box. Power-factor correction capacitors hold charge and must be discharged and shorted; a variable-frequency drive holds its d.c. link for some time after isolation; UPS and battery-backed control supplies inside the panel are fed from somewhere else entirely and do not die with the busbar; and a spring-charged breaker mechanism holds mechanical energy that will slam a linkage shut on a hand. On HV, the earths are what turn an inadvertent re-energisation from a fatality into a trip.

ul: Giving four or six steps when the question says five.
Treating 'dead switchboard' as a fact given by the question rather than a state to be established.
Relying on an indicator lamp, a panel voltmeter or a breaker position flag as proof of dead.
Proving the detector before the test and not after it.
Missing a back-feed - the emergency switchboard interconnector, a shore supply, a shaft generator, or the low-voltage side of a transformer.
Forgetting stored energy: capacitors, VFD d.c. links, UPS and battery supplies, and charged breaker springs.
Forgetting that the adjacent sections are live.
Cleaning with compressed air or water.
Letting someone other than the person who fitted a lock remove it.
Removing earths before the permit is closed, or letting anyone but the permit holder remove them.
Energising the busbar with outgoing breakers closed, or restoring the whole board at once.
Declaring the board operational without proving the emergency generator auto-start and the emergency switchboard changeover.
Calling the ISM Code's divisions 'regulations'. It has elements and paragraphs.

blocks.p:
"The breaker is racked out and the lamp is off. Is it dead?" No. Racking out removes one supply and the lamp proves nothing - lamps fail dark. It is dead when it has been proved dead at the point of work with a proved instrument, on all phases and to earth, after every source including back-feeds has been isolated.

"Why earth a high-voltage board you have already proved dead?" Because proving dead is a measurement taken at one instant, and the earth is a protection that lasts for the whole job: if the circuit is inadvertently re-energised, the earth turns a fatal contact into a fault the protection clears.

"Who may remove the earths?" The permit holder, and the removal is recorded. Not the duty engineer, not the person restoring power, and not before the permit is closed.

"You have restored the board. What proves the job is finished?" Not the lights coming on. The recorded insulation readings, the protection function tests against the approved setting schedule, the emergency generator auto-start and the emergency switchboard changeover.

ul: What is the safe isolation sequence? Identify, isolate every source, secure by locking and tagging, prove dead with a proved instrument, and earth where required.
What is prove-test-prove? Prove the detector on a known live source, test the conductors, prove the detector again.
Name three back-feeds into a main switchboard section. The emergency switchboard interconnector, a shore supply, and the low-voltage side of a transformer - plus a shaft generator or the bus-tie.
What is high voltage on a ship? Generally systems exceeding 1,000 V under class rules, requiring a separate permit, a person appointed in writing as competent, and mandatory earthing.
What is a sanction to test? The separate authorisation covering testing that requires the earths to be removed, with its own sign-off.
In what order do you close a permit? Persons out, tools tallied, earths off by the permit holder, covers on, recipient signs complete, issuer cancels, then locks and tags off by whoever fitted them.
How do you energise? Busbar first with all outgoing breakers open, check voltage, frequency, phase sequence and insulation monitoring, then feeders progressively with the largest last.
Which ISM elements are engaged? 6 resources and personnel, 7 shipboard operations, 8 emergency preparedness, 10 maintenance, 12 company verification and review.

blocks.p: Limb (a) is one word per step: ISOLATE - LOCK - PROVE - EARTH - CONTROL (steps 1 to 5). Limb (b) is ISSUE then CANCEL, and the order inside cancel is PEOPLE - TOOLS - EARTHS - COVERS - SIGN - LOCKS (steps 6 and 7). Limb (c) is CHECK IT, THEN WAKE IT - verification before energising, busbar before feeders, and the emergency systems proved last (steps 8 and 9).

ul: ISM Code Part A - element 6 resources and personnel and familiarisation; element 7 procedures for key shipboard operations concerning safety; element 8 emergency preparedness; element 10 maintenance of the ship and equipment; element 12 company verification, review and evaluation. The Code has elements and paragraphs, not regulations.
Flag State code of safe working practice - electrical work, permit to work, the prohibition on live working save in defined circumstances, proving dead, and stored energy.

Classification-society rules for electrical installations and high-voltage systems - the general treatment of systems above 1,000 V as high voltage, earthing facilities and interlocks on HV switchgear.
SOLAS chapter II-1 - main and emergency sources of electrical power, the emergency switchboard and its interconnection. Cited by concept in the restoration limb.
STCW 1978 as amended - management-level competence in the maintenance and repair of electrical and electronic control equipment, including isolation before work is permitted.

The Company's own SMS permit form is the controlling document for the permit's format, validity and signatures. The approved relay setting schedule and the maker's manual are the controlling documents for protection verification.

blocks.p: Three limits are declared. The high-voltage threshold is a class and national matter, not an IMO one: systems above 1,000 V are generally treated as high voltage under class rules, but the figure and its consequences are society-specific and the answer attributes it rather than asserting it universally. The permit's form, validity period and signature requirements are set by the Company's Safety Management System; the answer states the elements any competent permit must carry and makes the ship's own SMS controlling. Protection settings, interlocks, earthing facilities and the presence of a preferential trip or load-shedding scheme are installation-specific, so the answer says what must be verified and against which document, and asserts no setting. The isolation and restoration sequences themselves are declared as established electrical safe-working practice, because no international instrument prescribes them.

steps.title: Isolate - and find every source of supply
points: identify the section from the single-line diagram, not by eye
open and rack out or withdraw the incoming breaker
hunt the back-feeds: other generators and bus-tie, shore supply, emergency switchboard interconnector
shaft generator, transformer low-voltage back-feed
separately fed control, heater, UPS and battery supplies inside the panel
every isolation listed on the isolation schedule

steps.title: Lock off, tag and hold the key
points: each isolation locked in the open or withdrawn position
danger notice naming the permit, the work and the person
one key, held by the permit holder
only the person who applied a lock removes it
busbar shutters locked, breaker padlocked in test or isolated position

steps.title: Prove dead - and prove the instrument that proves it
points: approved voltage detector rated for the system
prove - test - prove, on a known live source or approved proving unit
all phases to each other and every phase to earth
test at the point of work
never accept an indicator lamp, panel voltmeter, position flag or somebody's word

steps.title: Earth, and discharge the stored energy
points: on HV apply the earthing switch or portable earths after proving dead
earths applied and removed only by the permit holder, and recorded
discharge and short power-factor correction capacitors
discharge the d.c. link of any variable-frequency drive
isolate UPS and battery-backed control supplies that do not die with the busbar
discharge the closing and tripping springs of a spring-charged mechanism

steps.title: Control the space, the tools and the person
points: screen or barrier every adjacent live section and mark the safe working limit
arc-rated clothing, face shield, insulating gloves and mat; no rings, watches or chains
insulated tools, tallied in and out
vacuum and lint-free cloths with an approved non-conductive cleaner
never water and never compressed air
never work alone - a competent standby who can isolate and resuscitate
ask him to repeat the brief back

steps.title: Issuing the permit
points: risk assessment or job safety analysis, then a toolbox talk
issued by the Chief Engineer or the SMS-authorised person to a named competent recipient
states equipment, limits of work, isolations, precautions, PPE, what stays live, validity
recipient signs to accept and inspects the isolations himself
displayed at the work site and on the permit board; bridge and duty engineer informed
HV: separate permit, person appointed in writing, mandatory earthing, sanction to test
time-limited - re-validated or re-issued, suspended if conditions change

steps.title: Closing the permit
points: all persons withdrawn and accounted for by name
tools, test leads, rags and materials removed and tallied
temporary earths removed by the permit holder and recorded
covers, shrouds, barriers and screens replaced
recipient signs the work complete and declares it safe to re-energise
issuer signs the permit cancelled, then locks and tags off by whoever fitted them
filed as an SMS record, entered in the PMS and reviewed

steps.title: Verification before anything is energised
points: reassembled to the maker's arrangement, no foreign object, tool tally reconciled
busbar and cable connections torqued to the specified value
insulation resistance phase to phase and phase to earth, compared with previous values
earth continuity and bonding restored, earth fault monitoring proved
relay settings verified against the approved setting schedule and discrimination study
function-test over-current, reverse power, under-voltage release, preferential trip, interlocks
test the automatic changeover to the emergency switchboard

steps.title: The power-restoration sequence
points: confirm the permit closed, earths off, locks off, space clear
inform the bridge and duty engineer, agree timing, log it
energise the busbar with every outgoing breaker open; check voltage, frequency, phase sequence, insulation monitoring
close feeders progressively, essential first and largest last, watching current, sound, smell and vibration
thermographic or temperature check on the disturbed joints once loaded
restore the interconnector and prove emergency generator auto-start, emergency lighting, steering gear and fire pumps
update the PMS, inform the Company, arrange class attendance where a class item was touched

questions.understand_first: The word to distrust in this question is dead. It sounds like a description of the switchboard, and it is really a claim about it - one that has to be earned, at the exact place a hand is going to go, moments before it goes there. A switch in the off position tells you what somebody intended, not what is true; a lamp that is not lit tells you nothing at all, because a broken lamp and a safe conductor look identical. So the first job is to hunt down every route by which electricity could arrive, and the surprising ones are the ones that hurt people - the emergency board that can push power backwards down the same cable it normally takes power from, a transformer fed from its far side, a small control supply inside the cabinet that comes from somewhere else entirely and never noticed the main breaker opening. Then you make your claim true, and you keep it true, because a measurement is a snapshot and a job lasts hours: that is what the locks and, on the big systems, the earths are for. The second thing worth holding is that the ship cannot go dark so that one cupboard can be cleaned. The panel beside the one he is working in is carrying everything the ship is doing, which is why so much of the briefing is about barriers, insulated tools counted in and out, and never blowing dust around with an air line. And the last idea is that finishing is a formal act, not a feeling. The paperwork closes in a fixed order, and the board is not working because the lights came back on - it is working because the insulation was measured, the protection was proved to still be set the way the ship's designers intended, and the emergency arrangements were shown to start when the main ones stop.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the five-step safe isolation sequence for a switchboard.
retrieval_cards.answer: Isolate every source of supply including back-feeds; lock off and tag with one key held by the permit holder; prove dead with a proved instrument on all phases and to earth at the point of work; earth on high voltage and discharge all stored energy; then control the space, the tools and the person.
retrieval_cards.why: Isolate - Lock - Prove - Earth - Control.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is prove-test-prove, and why is the last step the important one?
retrieval_cards.answer: Prove the voltage detector on a known live source or approved proving unit, test the conductors, then prove the detector again. The last step catches a detector that failed between the first proof and the test - which would otherwise read dead on live conductors.
retrieval_cards.why: An indicator lamp fails dark, which is why it is never accepted as proof.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the back-feeds that can re-energise an isolated switchboard section.
retrieval_cards.answer: The other generators through the bus-tie, a shore supply, the emergency switchboard interconnector, a shaft generator, the low-voltage side of a transformer, and separately fed control, heater, UPS and battery supplies inside the panel itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does stored energy hide in a switchboard after isolation?
retrieval_cards.answer: In power-factor correction capacitors, in the d.c. link of a variable-frequency drive, in UPS and battery-backed control supplies that do not die with the busbar, and in the charged closing and tripping springs of the breaker mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What differs about a high-voltage Permit to Work?
retrieval_cards.answer: Systems generally taken under class rules as exceeding 1,000 V need a separate HV permit; work is authorised only for a person appointed in writing as competent for high voltage; earthing is mandatory and recorded; and testing requiring the earths off is governed by a separate sanction-to-test document.
retrieval_cards.why: Earthing lasts the whole job, whereas proving dead is a measurement at one instant.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what order is a Permit to Work closed?
retrieval_cards.answer: All persons withdrawn and accounted for; tools and materials removed and tallied; temporary earths removed by the permit holder and recorded; covers, barriers and screens replaced; the recipient signs the work complete; the issuer signs the permit cancelled; and only then are locks and tags removed, each by the person who fitted it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must be verified before the board is energised?
retrieval_cards.answer: Reassembly with the tool tally reconciled and connections torqued to the specified value; insulation resistance phase to phase and to earth, compared with previous readings; earth continuity, bonding and earth fault monitoring; and protection relay settings against the approved setting schedule, with over-current, reverse power, under-voltage release, preferential trip and interlocks function-tested.
retrieval_cards.why: A loose joint is the classic cause of a switchboard fire, and a quietly altered relay setting only shows up on the day of a real fault.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is power restored, and what proves the job complete?
retrieval_cards.answer: Inform the bridge and log it; energise the busbar with every outgoing breaker open and check voltage, frequency, phase sequence and insulation monitoring; close feeders progressively with the largest last, watching current, sound and smell; take a temperature check on disturbed joints under load; then prove the emergency generator auto-start, the emergency switchboard changeover, emergency lighting, steering gear and fire pumps.
retrieval_cards.why: The lights coming on is not the proof; the recorded tests are.
