blocks.h: (a) Joining a ship with a record of port State control failures
1. What I establish before I hold the meeting

blocks.p: A meeting held on impressions achieves nothing. Before I speak I read: the previous inspection reports and the deficiency codes, so I know what actually recurred rather than what people say recurred; the outstanding non-conformities, observations and internal audit findings; the planned maintenance system and its overdue list; the Conditions of Class and outstanding statutory items; the record books - oil, garbage, rest hours; and the handover notes of my predecessor. Repeated failure is almost never a series of unrelated defects. It is one system failing repeatedly, and the pattern is visible in the codes.

blocks.h: 2. The initial meeting - what is said, and how

blocks.p: I hold it early, with all engine department officers and ratings together, and the Master informed and preferably present for the opening. The general procedure follows the shape the Safety Management System already prescribes for shipboard meetings:

ul: State the position honestly and without blame. The record is a fact; the purpose of the meeting is what we do next. Opening by looking for the person responsible closes the reporting culture on the first day.

Familiarisation first. Under the ISM Code the Company must ensure new personnel are properly familiarised - so I confirm that mine has happened and that theirs has, and that everyone can find and use the SMS procedure for his own job.
Name the recurring findings from the reports and ask the department why each recurs. The people who work the machinery usually know, and have often said so before without being heard.

Fix the routes for information - daily work planning, the pre-job toolbox talk, the watch handover, the defect report, the near-miss report, the safety committee meeting, and the direct route to me and to the Master.
Set the standard - what will be reported, to whom, in what form and by when - and record the meeting as an SMS document with actions, owners and dates.

blocks.h: 3. The flow of information after the meeting

blocks.p: The meeting establishes the channels; the channels must then work in both directions and be closed out. Downward: Company instructions, circulars and lessons learned, briefed and not merely posted. Upward: defect reports, near misses, non-conformities and suggestions, each acknowledged and answered - an unanswered report is the last report a man makes. Horizontally: watch handovers, deck-and-engine coordination and the permit system. And out to shore: the reporting line to the Company and the Designated Person's direct access to the highest level of management, which exists precisely so that a shipboard concern cannot be filtered out on the way up. Everything material is recorded, because the ISM Code obliges the Company to report, investigate and analyse non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences and to implement corrective action - and because on the next inspection, records are what will be examined.

blocks.h: 4. Examples of the repeated failures such a ship carries

blocks.p: The deficiencies that recur where the safety management system is weak are recognisable, and they are systemic rather than technical:

ul: Maintenance backlog - overdue planned maintenance jobs closed on paper, and machinery kept running past its interval.
Emergency equipment - emergency generator failing to start on load, emergency fire pump unable to deliver, quick-closing valves and remote stops seized, fire dampers and self-closing doors defective.
Pollution prevention - oily water separator with a defective 15 ppm alarm or stopping device, oil record book entries inconsistent with tank soundings, garbage management not followed.
Records and documentation - rest-hour records that are always exactly compliant, unsigned or retrospectively completed logs, missing test records.
Drills and familiarisation - drills recorded but not conducted, or conducted without briefing or debrief; new joiners not familiarised.
Permit systems - enclosed-space entry and hot-work permits issued as paperwork after the job rather than as control before it.

ISM implementation itself - which is what turns a list of individual deficiencies into a detainable ISM-related finding: the same defect recurring shows the system is not detecting, correcting or preventing.

blocks.h: 5. Effective communication with a multinational crew

ul: Establish the working language and require it for all safety-related communication - the ISM Code requires personnel to be able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties.

Close the loop. Instructions are repeated back, not nodded at. A nod is a cultural response as often as it is comprehension, and in some cultures a junior will not contradict a senior even when he knows the senior is wrong. That is a safety problem before it is a politeness problem.
Show, do not only tell. Demonstrate the job, walk the line, point at the valve. Physical demonstration crosses a language barrier that words do not.
Use visual aids - marked-up diagrams, colour-coded systems, photographs in the procedure, pictorial checklists at the machine.
Check comprehension by asking open questions - 'show me what you will do first' - never 'do you understand?', which has one answer everywhere in the world.
Toolbox talk before every non-routine job, with everyone present who will touch the job, including the ratings.

Build the reporting culture deliberately. Thank the man who reports a defect, in front of others; never punish the messenger. Port State control performance is a downstream measure of whether defects get reported early enough to be fixed.
Watch for fragmentation by nationality at meals and in leisure, mix the work teams deliberately, and apply one standard of behaviour to everyone.

blocks.h: 6. How a shore-office instruction is best utilised

blocks.p: A circular that is filed has changed nothing. The instruction is turned into shipboard action in six steps: read it and establish what it actually requires and by when; assess it against this ship, because a fleet instruction is written for a fleet and this ship's plant may differ; brief it at the safety meeting or toolbox talk in the working language, explaining why as well as what, because a reason is what survives; convert it into the ship's own routine - a planned maintenance job, a checklist item, a permit condition, an amended procedure - so that it outlives the people who heard the briefing; assign an owner and a date and verify that it was done, not that it was circulated; and report back to the office with the evidence and, where the instruction does not fit the ship, say so with reasons rather than silently not complying. Used that way the shore instruction becomes part of the plan-do-check-act loop that the safety management system is supposed to be; filed unread, it becomes the next non-conformity.

Diagnose before prescribing - apathy is a symptom, and the cause is usually lower down than encouragement can reach. Start with the material conditions, which are also legal entitlements under the MLC 2006: rest hours as actually worked rather than as recorded - a record that is always exactly compliant is a warning, not a reassurance - watch patterns and port workload, food, accommodation, and whether wages, relief and repatriation are certain. Uncertainty about going home is one of the strongest demotivators at sea and is not fixed by exhortation. Then delegate real responsibility with the authority to match it - give an engineer ownership of the purifiers or the boiler and let him report on them - credit him publicly and in the appraisal, plan on-board training and prepare juniors for their next certificate. And lead by example: turn out at three in the morning, wear the protective equipment you demand, and apply the same standard to everyone.

The task is not to erase difference but to stop it becoming misunderstanding or division. Set one visible standard of work, safety and behaviour and apply it identically regardless of nationality, rank or age - perceived favouritism destroys morale faster than anything else. Fix communication first, using the working language and read-back. Use the structured briefing, so every attitude receives the same information and the same opportunity to object. Deal with conflict early, privately and factually, separating the behaviour from the person, and treat bullying, harassment and discrimination as a formal matter through the on-board complaint procedure rather than as a personality clash. Mix the teams deliberately, pair experience with inexperience, and adjust your own style - direct instruction where a job is safety-critical, consultation where the man doing the work knows more about it than you do.

blocks.h: 9. Constructive competitiveness, and the framework this sits inside

blocks.p:
Read competitiveness as constructive competition - measurable improvement against a target and against the department's own past - and not as rivalry between individuals, which damages the teamwork safety depends on. Make performance visible and measurable: fuel and lubricating-oil consumption against the shop trial, generator running hours in port, planned-maintenance completion and overdue count, spares stock accuracy, unplanned stoppages. Set targets that belong to the department, not to a person - a month with no overdue jobs, a clean unannounced inspection - and benchmark against the sister ship or the fleet, because competing with another ship unites a department while competing with each other divides it. Recognise promptly and by name. And guard the limit: never let competition encourage short cuts, under-reporting of defects or falsified records - a department that competes on how few defects it reports is more dangerous than one that reports many, and on a ship with this history that is exactly the failure to avoid.

None of this is merely good practice. The obligations are real: the ISM Code requires competent manning, familiarisation, identified training needs, effective communication and the reporting and analysis of non-conformities; STCW as amended by the Manila amendments makes leadership, teamworking and managerial skill an examinable management-level competence for a Chief Engineer; the MLC 2006, with its 2022 amendments in force, makes the material conditions entitlements rather than favours; and the flag State - in India, under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 - enforces the result.

Limb (a) is one long sentence containing four separate demands, and it is worth 10 marks: the information-flow procedures at the initial meeting, examples of the repeated failures, communication with a multinational crew, and the use of a shore-office instruction. Each is almost certainly worth around two and a half marks, so each needs its own heading. The commonest failure is a good essay on port State control that never reaches the multinational limb or the shore-instruction limb at all. Limb (b) is worth 6 and has three named issues - motivation, attitude, competitiveness - so give three short blocks, not one.

blocks.h: The insight that turns this from a list into an answer

blocks.p: Repeated failure is one system failing repeatedly, not many unrelated defects. A ship that fails once has a defect; a ship that fails regularly has a safety management system that is not detecting, correcting or preventing - which is why inspectors escalate from individual deficiencies to an ISM-related finding, and why that finding is the one that detains. Say this early. It explains why the answer starts with information flow rather than with machinery, and it is the reason the examiner has joined 'failing PSC inspections' to 'poor safety management system implementation' in the same sentence.

Three different things, and the difference is what the ship on this record has never grasped. Correction fixes the defect in front of you. Corrective action removes the cause of a defect that has been detected, so that one does not come back. Preventive action removes the cause of a potential defect, before anyone has seen it. The whole distinction between the second and third is one word - detected against potential. A ship that only ever does correction will fail inspection after inspection while honestly believing it has fixed everything.

blocks.h: Why 'do you understand?' is the wrong question

blocks.p: It has one answer in every language and every culture. Replace it with an open, task-based question: show me what you will do first, which valve will you shut, what will you do if the pressure does not fall. Combine that with read-back of instructions and with physical demonstration, and you have crossed the language barrier without insulting anyone. This matters more than it sounds: in a number of cultures a junior will not contradict a senior even when he knows the senior is wrong, so the absence of an objection is not agreement - and on a ship that is a safety defect, not a courtesy.

blocks.h: A shore instruction is an input, not an outcome

blocks.p: The examiner's word is utilised. Circulating an instruction is not utilising it. The full-mark answer converts it into something the ship will still be doing in six months - a planned maintenance job, a checklist line, a permit condition, an amended procedure - with an owner, a date and a verification, and reports back with evidence. And it includes the honest half: where the instruction does not fit this ship's plant, say so with reasons. Silent non-compliance is how the next non-conformity is written.

ul: Answering only the PSC part and never reaching the multinational or shore-instruction limbs. Four demands, ten marks.
Inventing a real company's detention history or quoting inspection statistics. The scenario supplies the premise; do not manufacture evidence for it.
Opening the initial meeting by looking for who is to blame. It closes the reporting culture on the first day, which is the one thing the answer cannot afford.
Giving technical examples only. The repeated failures on such a ship are systemic - backlog, records, drills, familiarisation, permits.
Calling the ISM Code's divisions 'regulations'. It has elements and paragraphs; regulation is SOLAS's unit.
Treating communication as translation. It is working language plus read-back plus demonstration plus comprehension checking.
Asking 'do you understand?'
Filing the shore instruction rather than converting it into a routine with an owner and a date.
Reading 'competitiveness' as rivalry between individuals. On a ship that damages the teamwork safety depends on.
Forgetting that competition can suppress defect reporting - which on this ship would make the record look better and the ship more dangerous.

blocks.p:
"Why do inspectors treat the same deficiency recurring as worse than a new one?" Because a new deficiency is a defect, and a recurring one is evidence that the safety management system is not working - which is an ISM-related finding and a different order of seriousness.

"Your crew all nodded at the briefing and then did it wrong. What went wrong?" The briefing was never received. A nod is not comprehension; read-back and an open task-based question are. Deliver it again with a demonstration.

"The office sends an instruction that will not work on your plant. What do you do?" Reply with reasons and propose the equivalent measure that achieves the same object on this ship. Neither comply blindly nor stay silent - both end as non-conformities.

"Your department has reported far more defects since you joined. Is that a bad sign?" No, it is the first good one. Rising defect reports with falling repeat findings is exactly the pattern you want; the reverse is the ship you inherited.

ul: Which ISM elements are engaged? 3 company responsibility, 4 the designated person, 5 the Master's overriding authority, 6 resources, personnel and familiarisation, 7 shipboard operations, 8 emergency preparedness, 9 reports and analysis of non-conformities, 10 maintenance, 11 documentation, 12 company verification and review.

What is the designated person for? To provide a link between the Company and those on board, with direct access to the highest level of management - so a shipboard concern cannot be filtered out on the way up.
Which resolution carries the PSC procedures? A.1185(33), adopted 6 December 2023 by the 33rd Assembly.
Give three systemic examples of repeated deficiencies. Maintenance backlog closed on paper, emergency generator failing to start on load, and rest-hour records that are always exactly compliant.
How do you check comprehension? An open, task-based question - show me what you will do first - never a yes-or-no question.
What makes competition dangerous on a ship? When it rewards a low defect count, because it suppresses reporting.
Which instrument makes leadership an examinable competence? STCW as amended by the Manila amendments, at management level for a Chief Engineer.

blocks.p: Limb (a) in four words, one per demand: MEETING - EXAMPLES - LANGUAGE - INSTRUCTION (steps 2 to 6, with step 1 the preparation that makes the meeting worth holding). Limb (b) is CONDITIONS - STANDARD - MEASURE: fix the material conditions before preaching motivation, apply one visible standard to every attitude, and compete against a number rather than against each other (steps 7 to 9).

ul: ISM Code Part A - elements 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12. Element 6 carries familiarisation and the requirement that personnel can communicate effectively; element 9 carries reports and analysis of non-conformities and corrective action. The Code has elements and paragraphs, not regulations.
Resolution A.1185(33), Procedures for Port State Control, 2023 - clear grounds, more detailed inspection, detention and release, and review.
SOLAS regulation I/19 and regulation XI-1/4 - control, and port State control on operational requirements.
STCW 1978 as amended - leadership, teamworking and managerial competences introduced by the Manila amendments; management level for a Chief Engineer.

MLC 2006 - hours of rest, wages, repatriation, accommodation, food and catering, medical care and the on-board complaint procedure. The 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024 and are in force at this sitting.
Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (India) - in force 15 March 2026, repealing the 1958 Act at section 324(1). The operative Indian statute at this sitting; named for the flag-State limb only.

blocks.p: Three limits are declared. No company, ship, fleet or inspection record is named or invented: the question supplies the premise of a poor record and the answer treats it as given, offering only generic and realistic deficiency categories - no detention statistic, no database figure, no operator. Regional memoranda of understanding differ in their inspection regimes, targeting factors and company-performance calculations and are revised periodically, so the answer refers to the regional regime generically and asserts no formula, band or figure. The 2022 amendments to the MLC 2006 are cited at regime level as in force at this sitting; no individual amended provision is quoted, so rely on the entitlement in general terms rather than on a specific paragraph. The management content in limb (b) rests on those obligations as management practice, not on the authority of any theory of motivation.

questions.understand_first: There is a single idea underneath the whole of this question, and it is that a ship which keeps failing is not unlucky. One failure is a broken thing. A pattern of failures is a ship where the information does not move - where somebody knew the emergency pump would not start, and either did not say so, or said so to someone who did nothing, or wrote it down somewhere nobody reads. That is why a new Chief Engineer's first move is not a tour of the machinery but a look at the paperwork and then a conversation, and why the conversation has to be held in a way that does not punish the first person to admit something. If the meeting opens with a search for who is at fault, everyone learns on day one that the safe thing is silence, and the pattern continues with a new name on the door. The multinational part is the same problem wearing different clothes. Information can fail to move because nobody sent it, but it can also fail because it was sent and not received - and a room full of people nodding is one of the most convincing ways in the world to look like communication while being none. Some of that is language; a lot of it is that in plenty of places it is simply not done to tell a senior he is wrong. So you stop asking questions that can be answered with agreement, and start asking ones that can only be answered with knowledge. The last piece, the instruction from the office, tests the same thing pointing the other way: information arriving from outside is equally useless until somebody turns it into a job with a name and a date on it. And the short second half is the human machinery that makes all of this run - which starts, unglamorously, with whether people have slept, been paid, and been told when they are going home.

blocks.h: 1. The trigger, and what two consecutive D ratings actually means

blocks.p:
Before drafting anything, the trigger must be stated correctly, because the question's premise is one year short of it. Under MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28.7, a plan of corrective actions is required where a ship is rated D for THREE consecutive years, or E in any one year. Two consecutive D ratings do not engage regulations 28.7 to 28.9. A ship in that position is one year away from a mandatory plan, and there is no sanction in regulation 28 itself - no detention, no fine, no certificate withdrawn.

That is not a reason to do nothing; it is the reason to do this now. A plan begun after the third D has one year of data behind it and almost no time to change the outcome, whereas a plan begun after the second D has a whole reporting year to work in. So the correct answer is: the plan below is drafted voluntarily now, in the form regulation 28.8 will require, so that if a third D occurs it is already written, already in the SEEMP and already running - and so that it prevents the third D instead.

blocks.h: 2. What regulation 28.8 requires, and who verifies it

blocks.p: Regulation 28.8 is not the plan itself; it is the documentary and submission limb. It requires that the SEEMP be reviewed to include the plan of corrective actions accordingly, and that the revised SEEMP be submitted for verification no later than one month after reporting the attained annual operational CII. Regulation 28.7 fixes the plan's object - to achieve the required annual operational CII, that is, a rating of C or better. Regulation 28.9 adds the obligation that the plan is duly undertaken, so it is not discharged by submission. The plan therefore lives in SEEMP Part III, the mandatory CII implementation plan, and is verified by the Administration or its recognized organization - which since the amendments in force on 1 August 2025 also audits SEEMP Part III at company level.

rows: Throughout the calendar year

Fuel oil consumption and distance data collected under regulation 27 to the IMO DCS. From 1 January 2026 at the enhanced granularity introduced by the 2025 amendments - consumption by consumer type, consumption when not under way, onshore power in kilowatt-hours, laden distance, and transport work.
Within three months of the year end
Attained annual operational CII calculated and reported. For calendar year 2025 that fell due by 31 March 2026.
On verification
Rating assigned against the required CII for the year, and the Statement of Compliance issued under regulation 6.
Within one month of reporting the attained CII
Regulation 28.8 deadline: the revised SEEMP, containing the plan of corrective actions, submitted for verification. On the 31 March example that is 30 April.
The following calendar year
The plan is implemented and monitored under regulation 28.9, with the effect visible only in the next year's attained CII.

blocks.p: Two consequences of that timetable are worth stating in the plan. First, the window is short: one month between reporting and submission, so the analysis has to be done before the reporting deadline, not after it. Second, the required CII tightens every year - the reduction factor Z against the 2019 reference line is 11 per cent for 2026, rising under resolution MEPC.400(83) to 13.625, 16.250, 18.875 and 21.500 per cent for 2027 to 2030 - so a plan that merely restores last year's performance will still fail.
A plan that opens with a list of measures is a shopping list, not a corrective action plan. The first section establishes where the rating is coming from, using the ship's own data:

ul: Decompose the attained CII by voyage, by leg and by condition - laden, ballast, at anchor, in port - because the metric for most ship types is a deadweight-based ratio of CO2 to distance, and it is punished by idle time and by ballast passage regardless of how efficiently the machinery is running.
Separate consumption by consumer - main engine, auxiliary engines, boilers - which the enhanced IMO DCS granularity now makes routine rather than exceptional.
Compare against the shop trial and the model test: speed-power performance, specific fuel consumption, and the deterioration since the last dry docking.
Identify hull and propeller condition from performance monitoring - added resistance shows as increased power for the same speed - and the date of the last cleaning and coating.
Identify the commercial pattern: waiting time at anchor, ballast ratio, cargo utilisation, and the speeds actually ordered.

blocks.p: The diagnosis decides which of the following measures belong in this ship's plan. Each measure entered carries an owner, a target, a cost and a date.

ul: Hull and propeller. Hull cleaning and propeller polishing to a condition-based interval driven by performance monitoring rather than the calendar; a high-performance or foul-release coating at the next docking; and hull roughness measurement.

Propulsive efficiency devices. Propeller retrofit or re-pitching to the ship's actual operating profile rather than the design one; pre-swirl and post-swirl devices, propeller boss cap fins, rudder bulb and thrust fins.
Hull form. Bulbous bow modification where the ship consistently trades at a draught and speed far from those she was designed for - common after years of slow steaming.

Machinery. Main engine part-load optimisation and turbocharger cut-out; auxiliary engine load management and right-sizing; variable-frequency drives on sea water, cooling water and ventilation pumps and fans; LED lighting.
Energy recovery. Exhaust gas economiser and waste heat recovery; a shaft generator to remove auxiliary engines from the load at sea.

Larger interventions where the payback and the rating trajectory justify them - air lubrication, wind-assisted propulsion, battery hybridisation, shore power capability, and ultimately alternative fuel conversion.

Keep EEXI separate. The attained EEXI is a design requirement under regulation 23 and is already met; engine or shaft power limitation is not a corrective action for an operational rating, though its effect on the operating profile must be accounted for.

Speed management. Reducing service speed is the single most effective operational lever, because propulsive power varies roughly with the cube of speed - but it is the Company's and the charterer's decision, not the Chief Engineer's.
Voyage optimisation. Weather routeing, great-circle and current-assisted routeing, and minimising the distance actually steamed.

Just-in-time arrival. Steaming slowly to an agreed arrival slot rather than rushing to wait at anchor. This is the highest-value single change on most ships, because time at anchor produces emissions and no distance at all.
Trim and draught optimisation against the ship's own trim tables and, where available, a trim optimisation tool validated on measured data.
Ballast minimisation consistent with stability, propeller immersion and hull stress.
Autopilot and steering optimisation to reduce rudder movement and its added resistance.
Machinery load management in port - minimum generators on load, boiler and cargo-heating discipline, and shore power where fitted and available.

Performance monitoring and crew engagement - noon and continuous monitoring, a monthly review of the figures with the department, and training so that the men making the decisions can see their effect.

blocks.h: 7. Commercial measures, and the limit of the Chief Engineer's control

blocks.p: An honest plan says what the ship cannot fix by herself. The rating is driven substantially by decisions the ship does not make - the speed ordered, the ballast ratio, the cargo utilisation and the time spent waiting. On a time-chartered ship those belong to the charterer, which is why the industry developed contractual mechanisms such as the BIMCO CII Operations Clause for Time Charter Parties to allocate responsibility for the rating. The plan must therefore be a Company document with a shore owner, not an engine room document: it records which measures the ship controls, which the Company controls, which require charterer agreement, and which need capital approval and a docking window. A plan that assigns every action to the Chief Engineer is one that will not be delivered.

blocks.h: 8. Monitoring, verification, and the state of the measure itself

blocks.p:
The plan closes with its own control loop, in the SEEMP's plan - implement - monitor - self-evaluate and improve form: a defined baseline, a target attained CII for the coming year set against the required CII with the year's Z factor applied, quarterly review against that trajectory, named owners, and a documented escalation if the trajectory is not met. It is submitted to the Administration or recognized organization for verification, and since the 2025 amendments the Company's implementation of SEEMP Part III is itself subject to company audit.

Two currency points belong in the covering note. The measure is under review: regulation 28.11 required a review of the CII requirements to be completed by 1 January 2026, and its second phase - which expressly covers reinforced corrective action, enforcement and revision of the Z factor and reference lines - had opened but not concluded at this date. And the IMO Net-Zero Framework, approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, was not adopted: the extraordinary session convened to adopt it in October 2025 was adjourned to reconvene about twelve months later. Neither changes what regulation 28 requires today, and a plan written now should say so rather than anticipate either outcome.

The command verb is draft, and the two riders are timelines and examples of both technical and operational measures. So the answer must look like a document - sections, dates, owners - and it must give both kinds of measure, because giving only technical measures forfeits half of one of the three named demands. Sixteen marks with three demands means roughly a third each to the regulatory frame and timeline, the technical measures and the operational measures, with the diagnosis and the monitoring loop as the framing that turns a list into a plan.

blocks.h: The premise is one year short of the regulation, and saying so is the highest-value sentence on the paper

blocks.p: Regulation 28.7 triggers on D for THREE consecutive years, or E in one year. The question says two. Two consecutive D ratings therefore do not engage regulations 28.7 to 28.9 at all. This is not a quibble and it is not a reason to refuse the question: the right response is to state the trigger correctly, place the ship one year short of it, and then draft the plan anyway - because a plan written after the second D has a full year to change the outcome, while a plan written after the third has almost none. An answer that silently accepts the premise cannot demonstrate that it knows the rule; an answer that corrects the premise and still delivers the deliverable demonstrates both.

blocks.h: Regulation 28.8 is the paperwork limb, not the plan

blocks.p: Candidates routinely attribute the whole scheme to 28.8. Keep the sub-paragraphs apart. 28.7 creates the obligation and fixes its object - a plan of corrective actions to achieve the required annual operational CII. 28.8 says where the plan goes and when: the SEEMP is reviewed to include it, and the revised SEEMP is submitted for verification no later than one month after reporting the attained annual operational CII. 28.9 requires the plan to be duly undertaken. 28.10 encourages incentives for ships rated A or B. And note what is absent: regulation 28 prints no sanction at all - no detention, no fine, no certificate withdrawn. The consequence is a plan in the SEEMP, and the real pressure is commercial.

blocks.h: Why the metric punishes things the engine room does not control

blocks.p: For most ship types the operational carbon intensity is measured as a deadweight-based ratio of CO2 emitted to distance sailed. Two consequences follow and both belong in the plan. Time at anchor is the worst possible state: the ship burns fuel for the auxiliaries and boilers and travels no distance, so every hour waiting makes the ratio worse. And a ballast passage counts its distance and its fuel but earns no cargo credit under the deadweight-based metric. That is why just-in-time arrival and the ballast ratio matter more than almost any machinery measure, and why the answer must say plainly that the speed ordered, the waiting time and the cargo pattern are charterer and Company decisions. The industry's contractual response to exactly this problem is why CII clauses exist in time charters.

The required CII tightens every year. The reduction factor Z against the 2019 reference line runs 5 per cent for 2023, 7 for 2024, 9 for 2025 and 11 for 2026, and resolution MEPC.400(83) of April 2025 extended it to 13.625, 16.250, 18.875 and 21.500 per cent for 2027 to 2030. So a corrective action plan that restores last year's performance still fails, because last year's performance is measured against a looser line. The plan's target must be set against next year's required CII, not against this year's attained one - and that single point separates a plan that works from one that reads well.

blocks.h: What is new at this sitting

blocks.p: Two changes make an answer written in 2026 different from one written in 2024. The amendments in force on 1 August 2025 require enhanced granularity in the IMO DCS from 1 January 2026 - fuel consumption by consumer type, consumption when not under way, onshore power taken in kilowatt-hours, laden distance, and transport work in tonne-miles, TEU-miles or passenger-miles - and they make SEEMP Part III subject to company audits by the Administration or a recognized organization. For a corrective action plan both matter directly: the diagnosis that used to require special measurement is now a by-product of mandatory reporting, and the plan is now audited at company level rather than merely filed.

ul: Accepting the two-year premise without noticing that the trigger is three consecutive D ratings or one E.
Attributing the trigger, the plan and the submission all to regulation 28.8. It is 28.7 that triggers, 28.8 that submits, 28.9 that requires the plan to be undertaken.
Saying a D rating leads to detention, a fine or a withdrawn certificate. Regulation 28 prints no sanction.
Writing a list of measures with no diagnosis, no owners, no costs and no dates - which is not a plan.
Giving only technical measures, or only operational ones. The question names both.
Setting the target against this year's attained CII rather than next year's required CII, which is tighter.
Confusing the SEEMP parts: Part I is the energy efficiency management plan, Part II the data collection plan, and Part III is where the CII implementation plan and this corrective action plan live.
Offering EEXI engine power limitation as a corrective action. EEXI is a design requirement under regulation 23 and is a different obligation.
Quoting a percentage saving for a coating, a propeller device, air lubrication or trim optimisation. They are hull-form, draught and trade specific.
Assigning every action to the Chief Engineer when the largest levers - speed, waiting time, ballast ratio, cargo utilisation - are commercial.
Writing the IMO Net-Zero Framework in as though it were adopted. At this sitting it was approved but not adopted.

blocks.p:
"You have had two D ratings. What does MARPOL require you to do?" Strictly, nothing under regulation 28.7 - the trigger is three consecutive D ratings or one E. What it requires is that you continue to collect and report data under regulation 27 and maintain SEEMP Part III. What prudence requires is the plan, now.

"Your ship is rated D and your machinery is in excellent condition. How?" Very easily. The metric divides emissions by distance on a deadweight basis, so a ship that spends weeks at anchor, sails in ballast, or is ordered to arrive early and wait will rate badly however well her engine is running. That is the criticism the regulation 28.11 review is examining.

"Who signs off the plan?" It goes into the SEEMP and the revised SEEMP is submitted for verification to the Administration or its recognized organization within one month of reporting the attained CII - and since the 2025 amendments the Company's implementation of SEEMP Part III is itself company-audited.

"What happens if you do nothing?" No penalty in regulation 28. But the rating is published, charterers screen on it, financiers and cargo owners ask for it, and the required line tightens every year - so the commercial consequence arrives long before any regulatory one.

ul: What triggers a plan of corrective actions? D for three consecutive years, or E in any one year - regulation 28.7.

What does regulation 28.8 require? That the SEEMP be reviewed to include the plan, and the revised SEEMP submitted for verification not later than one month after reporting the attained annual operational CII.
When is the attained CII reported? Within three months of the end of the calendar year.
Which SEEMP part carries it? Part III, the CII implementation plan.
What is Z for 2026? 11 per cent against the 2019 reference line, rising to 13.625, 16.250, 18.875 and 21.500 per cent for 2027 to 2030 under MEPC.400(83).
To what tonnage does regulation 28 apply? 5,000 gross tonnage and above.
Name two technical and two operational measures. Hull and propeller cleaning and a shaft generator; just-in-time arrival and trim optimisation.
What sanction does regulation 28 impose for a poor rating? None. The consequence is the plan and, commercially, the published rating.
What was the status of the IMO Net-Zero Framework? Approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 but not adopted - the extraordinary session convened in October 2025 adjourned.

blocks.p: The regulation in four numbers: 28.7 triggers, 28.8 submits, 28.9 does, 28.10 rewards - and 28.11 is the review of the whole thing. The plan in four words: DIAGNOSE - TECHNICAL - OPERATIONAL - COMMERCIAL, wrapped in the SEEMP's own plan, implement, monitor, self-evaluate cycle. The timeline in three numbers: three months to report, one month to submit, one year to show it worked.

questions.understand_first: The scheme this question sits in is simpler than its vocabulary. Every year a ship reports how much fuel she burned and how far she went, and from that a single number is worked out - roughly, the carbon she emitted per tonne of capacity per mile travelled. That number is compared against a line that was drawn from the whole world fleet's performance in one baseline year, and the line is dragged a little lower every year on purpose. Depending on which side of the line you fall, and by how much, you are given a letter from A to E. The letters are not decoration: fall far enough below often enough and you are required to write down what you are going to do about it, put that document inside the ship's energy management plan, and hand it to your flag State. Two things about this are worth understanding properly. The first is that the number is a ratio with distance on the bottom, which means the fastest way to look terrible is to sit still - a ship waiting at anchor burns fuel for her generators and boilers and covers no ground at all, so every day of waiting drags the figure down no matter how beautifully her engine is running. That is why so much of any real plan is about arriving when you are actually wanted rather than early, and why the biggest levers are held by the people who decide where the ship goes and how fast, not by the people who maintain her. The second is that the line moves. Getting back to the performance that was acceptable last year is not good enough, because this year's line is lower. A plan aimed at yesterday's standard fails on the day it succeeds.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What triggers a plan of corrective actions under MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 28.7: a rating of D for three consecutive years, or a rating of E in any one year. Two consecutive D ratings do not engage it.
retrieval_cards.why: A ship with two D ratings is one year short of the obligation, which is exactly why the plan is worth writing voluntarily then.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do regulations 28.7, 28.8, 28.9 and 28.10 each do?
retrieval_cards.answer: 28.7 creates the obligation and fixes its object - achieve the required annual operational CII. 28.8 requires the SEEMP to be reviewed to include the plan and the revised SEEMP submitted for verification not later than one month after reporting the attained CII. 28.9 requires the plan to be duly undertaken. 28.10 encourages incentives for ships rated A or B.
retrieval_cards.why: Attributing the whole scheme to 28.8 is the standard error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the two deadlines in the CII cycle.
retrieval_cards.answer: The attained annual operational CII is reported within three months of the end of the calendar year. The revised SEEMP containing the corrective action plan is submitted for verification not later than one month after that reporting.
retrieval_cards.why: So the analysis must be finished before the reporting deadline, not after it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What penalty does regulation 28 impose for a D or E rating?
retrieval_cards.answer: None. Regulation 28 prints no sanction - no detention, no fine and no certificate withdrawal. The regulatory consequence is a plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP; the real pressure is commercial, because the rating is published and charterers and financiers screen on it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can a ship in excellent mechanical condition still be rated D?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the metric is a deadweight-based ratio of CO2 to distance sailed. Time at anchor burns fuel and covers no distance, and a ballast passage earns no cargo credit - so waiting time, ballast ratio and ordered speed can produce a poor rating regardless of machinery condition.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the criticism the regulation 28.11 review is examining.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the reduction factor Z, and why does it matter to the plan's target?
retrieval_cards.answer: Z reduces the 2019 reference line: 5 per cent for 2023, 7 for 2024, 9 for 2025 and 11 for 2026, extended by MEPC.400(83) to 13.625, 16.250, 18.875 and 21.500 per cent for 2027 to 2030. Because the required CII tightens annually, a plan that merely restores last year's performance still fails.
retrieval_cards.why: Set the target against next year's required CII, not this year's attained one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give two technical and two operational measures for a corrective action plan.
retrieval_cards.answer: Technical: condition-based hull cleaning and propeller polishing with a foul-release coating at the next docking, and a shaft generator or waste heat recovery to unload the auxiliary engines at sea. Operational: just-in-time arrival instead of steaming fast to wait at anchor, and trim and draught optimisation against the ship's own tables.
retrieval_cards.why: No percentage saving is claimed for any of them - all are hull-form, draught and trade specific.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What changed for the IMO DCS and SEEMP Part III from the 2025 amendments?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution MEPC.385(81), in force 1 August 2025, requires enhanced reporting granularity from 1 January 2026 - fuel consumption by consumer type, consumption when not under way, onshore power in kilowatt-hours, laden distance and transport work - and makes SEEMP Part III subject to company audits by the Administration or a recognized organization.
retrieval_cards.why: The diagnosis that once needed special measurement is now a by-product of mandatory reporting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does SEEMP Part III sit, and what was the status of the Net-Zero Framework at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I is the energy efficiency management plan, Part II the fuel oil consumption data collection plan, and Part III is the mandatory CII implementation plan where the corrective action plan lives. The IMO Net-Zero Framework was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 but NOT adopted - the extraordinary session convened in October 2025 to adopt it was adjourned.
